title: Review: next-generation metal hydride systems for sustainable hydrogen storage—kinetics, nanostructuring, and intelligent materials discovery
abstract: Abstract Hydrogen is one of the major pillars of the low-carbon economy, but its wide application is limited by difficulties in storage. Metal hydrides (MHs) represent excellent candidates for storage since they are characterized by high volumetric density, reversibility, and safety. This article provides a thorough and integrative review of novel generation MH storage technologies based on intermetallic, complex, magnesium, and chemical hydrides with special focus on thermodynamics and kinetics of these processes. Major restrictions, including high temperatures of desorption, slow kinetics, and cycling instability, are discussed in conjunction with current advanced approaches to address the issue of MH properties improvement, such as catalyst addition, nanoscale modifications, composite materials, and HEA engineering. Special attention is paid to innovative HEA materials, which can improve hydrogen mobility and binding energies due to composition engineering and lattice distortion. In addition, a rapid growth in the use of artificial intelligence algorithms for the fast development of new materials with tailored features and accurate hydrogen storage property prediction is described. Relevance to practice is supported by examples involving hydrogen fuel cells for transport and space applications. Although MH-based storage technologies still have certain drawbacks, such as heat management, material stability, and environmental aspects, they have great promise as reliable and scalable platforms for hydrogen storage.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The fast climate impacts require a global transition to clean and sustainable energy storage. Fossil fuels are the drivers of energy and greenhouse gas emissions, which contribute to climate change, warming, and weather events [ 1 ]. The application of fossil fuels also leads to the exhaustion of non-renewable resources and environmental concerns, which emphasize the need for a transition to hydrogen energy [ 2 ,  3 ]. Hydrogen is a versatile and high-energy–density carrier that produces only water when consumed and can assist in the transition of the industrial, transportation, and aviation sectors to a low-carbon economy. Governments and corporations are investing in hydrogen to combine with renewable energy in a “hydrogen economy,” in which hydrogen is a supplementary energy source to electricity [ 4 ]. Figure  1  illustrates the present global application of hydrogen-based fuel, which supports sustainable development because hydrogen can be produced from renewable materials such as water and biomass [ 5 ]. Hydrogen also has significant promise, but storage limitations are also a crucial issue in creating energy transitions associated with climate change. The efficiency of H 2  fuel use is shown in Fig.  2 . This is due to the light gaseous nature of the hydrogen at ambient temperature, which complicates safe and efficient storage and transportation processes [ 7 ]. Without the development of storage technologies, the scalability of hydrogen as a green energy vector will be limited, and thus it will be difficult to achieve the objectives related to climate. Boil-off losses are related to liquid hydrogen, contribute to energy wastefulness, and can increase carbon emissions unless properly managed [ 8 ,  9 ]. Different technologies of storage are depicted in Fig.  3 . Increasing storage technology is also critical in environmental sustainability, as it will decrease fossil fuel consumption and minimize global warming. Figure 2 Uses of hydrogen as fuel. Based upon the climate call, a review of the current classifications of hydrogen storage technologies is in order, as these modalities provide the foundation for the implementation of a hydrogen-based energy system (Table  1 ). Hydrogen storage technologies can be broadly classified as physical storage solutions or chemical solutions, and each type of solution has different advantages and weaknesses regarding efficiency, safety, and storage capacity. Physical solutions refer to the molecular confinement of hydrogen without any chemical binding, utilizing the principles of pressure, temperature, or adsorption to achieve higher densities. One of the most used physical solutions is compressed gas storage, where hydrogen is stored in high-pressure vessels (generally 350–700 bar) [ 8 ,  9 ,  27 ].

Researchers around the world agree that hydrogen’s low volumetric energy density at practical temperatures and pressures strongly contributes to metal-hydrogen interactions being required for practical storage applications. For this reason, choosing & developing viable metal hydrides is critical because they can store hydrogen in a compact, reversible, and stable format through chemisorption [ 28 ]. Table  2  outlines the main differences between the six most developed national green hydrogen strategies in order to understand how mature/ambitious they are and how successfully they are deploying their programmes (i.e., India, EU, USA, Japan, Australia and China). The only country that has just launched its hydrogen strategy is India, which launched its Green Hydrogen Mission in 2023 with a 5 MMT production goal by 2030 and is providing substantial funding through capital subsidies and its National Green Hydrogen Mission (which has 862,000 tonnes of production capacity currently allocated). In contrast, the EU has been developing its hydrogen strategy since 2020 for its own 40 GW by 2030 target and has proven the credibility of its policy by having two facilities currently under construction (2.84 GW total). The US is also developing its hydrogen strategy, which started in 2022, using tax credits under the Inflation Reduction Act in addition to establishing Regional Hydrogen Hubs to support hydrogen production at a target price of $1/kg; it currently has 1.74 GW of hydrogen production capacity in operation or under construction. Japan is the earliest commercial user of green hydrogen and has been since 2017. Its focus is on reducing the cost of green hydrogen to $3/kg and relying on international facilities for supply; therefore, it has only a moderately high regulatory level of credibility with a 15 GW worldwide deployment target. Australia has been attempting to establish itself as a future exporter of green hydrogen since 2019 with mega-project grant programs; however, as of mid-2022, it only has around 1 GW of existing capacity, and there is only 1 GW of capacity announced or under construction (as of July 2022). China has the most enforceability and industrial development, with a target of 100,000 to 200,000 tonnes of green hydrogen by 2025, as well as exceeding its target this year (2022) with an existing production capacity of 125,000 tonnes from completed projects. Examining the rest of the countries in the table, it can be seen that while the credibility and availability of funding (to develop green hydrogen projects) are highest in the EU and USA, the enforceability of binding mandates that would guarantee green hydrogen production capacity continues to be moderately low in most places. In addition to the above concerns, infrastructure alignment globally continues to be a challenge with existing production capacity far below the 2030 targets in all listed nations. The comparison shows that the regions of Asia (India, Japan and China) appear to be heavily focused on production and cost strategies, while the EU and USA lean toward innovation funding (in terms of research) and developing regional hubs for diversification. The results presented above indicate that stronger offtake (purchase) mandates and rapid infrastructure will need to be implemented to reach the global green hydrogen targets by 2030 [ 12 ].

Among these, metal hydrides have high volumetric storage density and reversible absorption/desorption properties. Examples: LaNi 5 , medium capacity, efficient at low temperature and pressure; MgH 2 , good reversibility and high weight percentage capacity (7.6 wt%, 110 g H 2 /L), the best onboard storage material [ 35 ]. Complex hydrides, such as LiBH 4  and Mg(BH 4 ) 2 , have theoretical capacities of 12 − 15 wt%, but high desorption temperatures and low kinetics make them unsuitable. AlH 3  and BeH 2  have very high hydrogen storage capacity (10 wt%, 18.2 wt%), but reversibility and toxicity are issues [ 36 ,  37 ]. Ammonia borane (AB) and AB/ionic liquid mixtures have potential for compact release but are not suitable for regeneration and cycling [ 38 ]. The gravimetric energy density of hydrogen is about 33.3 kWh/kg (120 MJ/kg), making it very attractive for use in applications where weight is a concern, such as transportation and aerospace, as well as portable power sources [ 39 ]. However, the final viability of any storage technology depends on the ability to achieve high energy density in conjunction with moderate temperatures of operation, fast kinetics, and good cycle durability, which is a complex task that continues to engage intense research and development efforts worldwide.
Novel ideas and strategies have been proposed to efficiently manage the release of hydrogen in various systems.

For example: Improving the hydrogen storage capacity by adding elements that produce fewer stable hydrides leads to an expansion of the hydrogenated system, which reaches thermodynamically stable conditions with ΔH values of 20–50 kJ/mol H 2  in Mg systems [ 40 ]. Smaller particle sizes lead to higher surface energy, which lowers enthalpy as excess surface energy is produced by heat. The stabilized Mg nanograins produce numerous grain boundaries, which provide plenty of excess enthalpy for various uses [ 41 ]. Studies on metastable phases increase the metal-hydrogen distance, which lowers coulombic attraction, decreases formation energy, and increases hydrogen mobility for improved interactions [ 42 ]. Surface catalysis is essential for H 2  chemisorption on doped metals. The breaking of H–H bonds requires ~ 432 kJ/mol. The Sabatier rule suggests that adsorption energies should be in the optimal middle range: too high prevents desorption into the Mg subsurface, while too low prevents initial H 2  adsorption. This balance optimizes catalyst performance [ 43 ]. The catalytic hydrogen production/storage processes are shown in Fig.  5 . In the case of catalyst doping and nanostructuring, both processes contribute to the hydrogen storage process through different effects. In terms of catalytic doping, the catalyst aids in increasing the reaction rate of the hydrogen storage process, such as dissociation, absorption, transfer, and nucleation through the use of the principle known as the Sabatier Principle to ensure the best binding to the hydrogen molecule. Figure 5 Overview of catalysts in hydrogen production. Reproduced from [ 44 ] under CC BY license.

These findings are further described in the following sections of this manuscript with particular reference to their implications for the storage of hydrogen in different metal hydrides (see Fig.  3  and Table  3 ). Metal hydrides are regarded as being optimal for hydrogen storage because they rapidly form hydrogen complexes, thus allowing regulation of storage and release kinetics. A significant number of hydride compounds of metals have been found to have desirable physicochemical properties, and quite a few show great promise in conventional storage applications. The natural inertness of the metal hydrides toward other materials makes them extremely reliable for commercial applications and lends them environmental safety. As a result, metal hydrides represent a great alternative to petroleum, diesel, and other natural gases to boot, thanks to their low mass. Accordingly, such hydrides may have advantages over competing storage media and promote hydrogen storage technology [ 35 ].

Categorically, three main categories of MHs exist: interstitial, complex, and nanostructured MH variants. Hence, different kinds of MH are being used:

1. Classical/Interstitial Hydrides  These include AB 5 - types (e.g., LaNi 5 ), AB-type (e.g., FeTi), AB 2 -type (Laves phase, e.g., ZrMn 2 ), A 2 B-type (e.g., Mg 2 Ni), AB 3 -type, and some solid solution alloys (e.g., V-based) [ 49 ,  50 ].

The prevalence of AB 5  alloy structures is because the rare-earth and d-block metal structure is present [ 51 ]. Most recent inventions in this field are partial replacements of elements with aluminum, cobalt, manganese, tin, or ruthenium, which change the plateau pressures, increase cyclic stability, and reduce degradation susceptibility [ 52 ,  53 ]. For instance, substituting Ni with Sn in LaNi 5  reduces the equilibrium pressure and speeds the adsorption rate. Alloying with Zr or Ce in AB 5  compounds enables high-pressure applications [ 54 ,  55 – 56 ].

Merits  The merits of interstitial metal hydrides for hydrogen storage stem from surface modification and nanostructuring, which optimize the particle size for improved diffusivity. This, in turn, yields excellent reversibility, faster kinetics, and low equilibrium pressures, as well as good resistance to impurities and enhanced cyclic stability (up to 1500 cycles) [ 51 ,  57 ].

Demerits  Although the major advantage lies in safer compressed gas storage, the demerits include a low gravimetric capacity (< 2 wt% for LaNi 5 H 6 ), high cost, complex activation, and limited hydrogen diffusivity, making it unsuitable for high-capacity vehicular needs specifically [ 58 ].

Complex Hydrides  These materials are lightweight (as shown in Table  4 ), which are alanates (e.g., sodium NaAlH 4 , lithium LiAlH 4 , calcium Ca(AlH 4 ) 2 , potassium KAlH 4 ), borohydrides (e.g., lithium LiBH 4 , zinc Zn(BH 4 ) 2 , sodium NaBH 4 , calcium Ca(BH 4 ) 2 ), nitrides (e.g., lithium Li 3 N), and metal ammine complexes (e.g., Mg(NH 3 )6Cl 2 ) [ 66 ].

These new metal hydrides exhibit nanoconfinements in scaffolds such as carbon tubes and carbon nanorods, which increase the surface energy while reducing the particle size, thereby enhancing their reversibility. Merits  They have high gravimetric and volumetric densities just like other metal hydrides, and they use abundantly light elements, offering cleaner energy release while being environmentally benign [ 68 ].

Demerits  While it does show high thermodynamic stability, for this it needs to be operated at elevated temperatures (> 473 K), which, on the contrary, reduce the kinetics and give poor reversibility; all this, coupled with it producing various by-products, makes it cost-ineffective as well as industrially nonviable [ 68 ].

Magnesium-based alloys  these include MgH 2  and alloys like Mg–Ni or Mg–Al, with body-centered cubic structures. Recent innovations in this field include alloying with Ni or rare-earth forms of nanostructures (e.g., ball milling, which reduces the particle size to < 10 nm), thereby improving kinetics. Catalyst doping and reactive composites lower desorption temperatures from 573 to 373 K. Amorphous Mg-alloys via melt-spinning enhance absorption rates [ 69 ].
Merits  High capacity (7.6 wt% for MgH 2 ), low cost, abundance, good volumetric density, and high reversibility [ 70 ].

Demerits  However, the merits of Mg-based alloys for hydrogen storage have been limited by their high desorption temperatures (> 573 K), which make the kinetics slower and reduce their resistance to oxidation. One of the major demerits of this system is embrittlement during cycling, which limits its practical use [ 71 ].

Chemical Hydrides  These materials provide a promising class of hydrogen storage, based on light elements (boron, nitrogen, hydrogen) rather than conventional metal hydrides. The chemical composition allows for higher capacities, usually above 10 wt%, and easier hydrogen release than other complex hydrides [ 72 ]. In contrast to reversible materials (intermetallics, alanates), chemical hydrides are usually irreversible, releasing hydrogen in non-cyclable reactions, but with high energy density and easier release conditions [ 73 ,  74 ].

Merits  High gravimetric hydrogen storage capacity: they are more suitable for use in places where weight becomes a critical factor (AB has a capacity of 19.6 wt.% hydrogen). Environmental stability: AB-type materials maintain stability at room temperature when exposed to air or basic to neutral aqueous environments; therefore, the storage and degradation of AB materials in time do not pose a significant hazard to the user [ 75 ]. Storage of higher energy densities for emergency power applications: The unique release profile of the hydrogen from AB materials is one-directional, resulting in their suitability for emergency power applications since they do not need to be recharged [ 76 ].

Demerits  Irreversibility: According to various resources, most of the chemical hydrides produced at a chemical plant (excluding complex or intermetallic hydrides) are non-recyclable, i.e., one-time-use fuels. Therefore, once the hydrogen is exhausted from these hydrides, the remaining product from the chemical hydride must be removed, and there will always be the costs involved with the removal and reprocessing of that material; as such, the operational complexity or the operational cost of obtaining hydrogen will rise as a result of this additional requirement to treat the spent product [ 77 ]. Environmental and safety issues associated with spent product management: The decomposition of AB systems generates hazardous by-products, including B 2 H 6 , which have the following effects: they lock up hydrogen, decrease efficiency, and can potentially pose environmental and/or health hazards; thus, some means of additional purification or containment would likely be required for all AB systems since these materials are often toxic, corrosive, or present hazards to the environment or human health [ 78 ]. The rate of hydrogen desorption is very low (< 100 °C) as there are large activation energy differences between the kinetic pathways and there are competing side reactions, which limit fuel cell applications at low temperatures. These constraints can be alleviated by using catalysts [ 79 ,  80 ]. Increased regeneration energy needs: The regeneration of by-products living in off-board units requires significant amounts of energy input, which may degrade the overall system efficiency and, consequently, the suitability of the materials for cyclic onboard vehicular deployment compared with reversible materials [ 81 ]. Following a detailed consideration of the main commercially feasible metal hydrides used for hydrogen storage, it appears that despite improvements such as nanostructuring, for storage capacity, kinetic characteristics and cost-effectiveness, intrinsic and persistent issues remain which limit their current environmental sustainability.

The aim of this work is to examine the transparency of various hydrogen storage materials, as well as the basic aspects of all systems supporting the advantages and disadvantages in terms of kinetics and thermodynamics. Within the scope of this paper, we also aim to explain practical examples and observations of pertain toward real-world implementations of hydrogen storage, and highlight the challenges and developments necessary in order to enable industry-scale, efficient hydrogen storage. A focus on gravimetric energy density alone does not afford a complete evaluation of the utility of hydrogen storage as a practice and offer little insight into the limitations of hydrogen storage, as it does not take into account volumetric issues and other relevant challenges, such as cost or speed of reaction. The research detailed here has examined hydrogen-related storage technologies, including their associated thermodynamics and kinetics, as well as their benefits and drawbacks. In addition, the review has provided several case studies that apply these technologies in practical situations. It also discusses ongoing issues related to the adoption of scalable and cost-effective hydrogen storage technology and highlights the technology’s successful demonstration in more recent developments.

The article is also an overview of fuel cells powered by hydrogen-based fuels that were put into service in some of the most recent fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs) (Toyota Mirai, Hyundai Nexo, BMW iX5 Hydrogen, and Honda CR-V e: FCEV) and a comparison of the various fuel cell systems used. In comparison with each other, all four vehicles have been evaluated in terms of their proton-exchange membrane fuel cell (PEMFC) system, fuel tank capacity, driving range, efficiency, and overall performance in “real-world” situations. Finally, the article reviews metal hydride hydrogen storage systems and their application by NASA, highlighting the ongoing research on metal hydride hydrogen storage systems to be used in the Artemis program and in manned spacecraft and lunar landers, as well as for future jobs with regenerative fuel cells to support long-duration lunar and Mars missions.

A comprehensive approach that connects material sciences to battery applications in vehicles and the latest space technology has created an integrated view of hydrogen storage’s role in supporting sustainable and ultimately low-carbon futures in land-based mobile equipment and space exploration.

sections.heading: Categorization of metal hydrides for hydrogen storage
paragraphs: Reversible hydrogen-storage metal hydrides are divided into two categories, dependent upon chemical composition and bonding properties. The primary ones are intermetallic hydrides, complex hydrides and elemental hydrides. Figure  7  summarizes the various classifications of hydrogen storage technologies. Figure 7 Mechanistic classification of hydrogen storage technologies. Reprinted from [ 82 ], with permission from Elsevier.

sections.heading: Intermetallic hydrides
paragraphs: Hydrogen atoms combine with intermetallic compounds, which are alloys made of two or more metals, to form intermetallic hydrides [ 83 ]. They consist of a single hydrogen-binding element (A) and a hydrogen-binding element (B) with a lower binding strength, creating intermediate hydrogen storage properties [ 84 ]. Intermetallic hydrides are extensively studied because of their outstanding hydrogen storage capacity, ease of manufacture, flexibility under thermodynamic conditions, active absorption/desorption rates, and extended life cycles [ 85 ]. The typical crystal structures of intermetallic hydrides are AB, AB 2,  and AB 5  [ 8 ]. Table  4  presents quantitative benchmarks for various metal hydrides.

AB-type Intermetallic Hydrides  The compounds were first discovered in 1958 and are mainly made of Ti, Zr (A elements), and Fe, Co, Ni (B elements) [ 8 ,  85 ,  86 ]. Utilization of AB-type hydrides offers value due to overall competitiveness in pricing (excluding cobalt) combined with the abundance of elements comprising the metals and their compounds. They allow hydrogen to be stored under moderately low temperature/pressure conditions (similar to ambient), thus providing for optimum criteria for both kinetics and capacity when hydrogen is released from these types of hydrides. However, the majority of AB-type compounds must first undergo elaborate activation protocols prior to their use as hydrogen storage materials, and they can also be poisoned easily due to impurities in reaction conditions; thus, there are limits to the effective use of AB-type compounds across the entire operating range of hydrogen pressures [ 87 ]. A representative example is TiFe, which is an inexpensive, abundant compound with strong cycling stability at low pressure and mild conditions [ 88 ].

AB 2 -type Intermetallic Hydrides (Laves phase)  These compounds consist of elements like Zr, Ti, Y, La for A, and V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Ni for B [ 83 ]. AB 2  hydrides offer high volumetric hydrogen capacities, rapid formation and breakdown rates, and simple activation processes. However, their cost of production may be high because the major constituents incorporated in their preparation are expensive. Compared to AB 5  compounds, AB 2 -type compounds have low contaminant resistance and decreased structural stability, such as ZrV 2 , ZrMn 2 , and TiMn 2  [ 8 ,  89 ].

AB 5 -type Intermetallic Hydrides  AB 5 -type compounds were discovered by van Vucht, Kuijpers and Bruning, and they react rapidly and reversibly with hydrogen. They are usually made of a ternary metal hydride compound of a rare-earth metal (A) and Ni or Co (B) [ 90 ]. AB 5  alloys, with a CaCu 5 -type structure, are recognized for their outstanding ability to absorb hydrogen, withstand cycles, and resist impurities, making them suitable for various applications [ 90 ]. There is a broad selection of substitutional alloys that can be added to the AB 5  phase, and hydrides can be developed to meet individual needs [ 8 ]. An intriguing application is their combination with proton-exchange membrane hydrogen fuel cells (PEMFCs) to provide hydrogen storage and a reliable power supply [ 8 ]. LaNi 5  is a potential example, which has a large volumetric capacity, high cycling stability, high gas impurity resistance, low operating temperature and pressure. However, low specific energy density, low hydrogen storage capacity (1.4 wt%), are expensive and flammable due to the non-abundance of rare-earth materials [ 88 ]. Intermetallic hydrides typically provide rapid and reversible hydrogen charging and discharging rates, high volumetric densities, and can be used at almost ambient temperature and pressure. Their usable hydrogen capacities are usually less than 2 wt% [ 84 ].

sections.heading: Complex hydrides
paragraphs: Complex hydrides are metal salts in which a hydrogen atom and a core atom are bonded in a complex of an anion due to directional covalent bonds [ 91 ]. The hydrogen in these crystalline compounds is covalently attached to core atoms in a complex anion that is, in turn, attached to a metallic cation [ 92 ]. Complex hydrides have much higher gravimetric hydrogen storage capacities, typically between 4 and 14 wt% [ 84 ,  93 ]. The alanates, borohydrides, and amides are the major hydrides in categories of complex hydrides of interest in hydrogen storage [ 8 ].

Alanates (Alumino-hydrides)  These are complex hydrides based on the Al element with four hydrogen atoms being covalently attached to an Al metallic cation, coordinating with an anion containing Al at its core [ 94 ]. Alanates include several different compounds, such as Na, lithium, Mg, potassium, calcium, and mixed metal alanates [ 8 ,  95 ]. The sodium aluminum hydride (NaAlH 4 ) is thoroughly studied, with a theoretical hydrogen content of 7.4 wt%. However, only a fraction of this hydrogen can be reversibly utilized. A major limitation is that for most alanates, the dehydrogenated compounds cannot be dehydrogenated under conditions suitable for practical applications, and the final desorption step often occurs at excessively high temperatures. Nevertheless, the potential of a stationary use is presented, assuming that the limitations of kinetics can be overcome [ 8 ].

Borohydrides  One of the most promising classes of materials to be used as high-capacity hydrogen storage materials is complex hydrides, which represent the highest known theoretical gravimetric hydrogen content of all solid-state systems [ 96 ]. A prominent example is that of lithium borohydride (LiBH 4 ), which can store up to 18.5 wt % hydrogen under ideal conditions [ 97 ]. In general, borohydrides are thermally stable compounds and therefore begin to release hydrogen only at higher temperatures [ 98 ]. Common representatives are sodium borohydride (NaBH 4 ), lithium borohydride (LiBH 4 ), magnesium borohydride (Mg(BH 4 ) 2 ) and calcium borohydride (Ca(BH 4 ) 2 ) [ 99 ]. Despite their huge storage capacity, borohydrides offer many practical drawbacks. They have a high hydrogen-metal bond strength, which leads to a high enthalpy of dehydrogenation, i.e., for LiBH 4 , a value of about 75 kJ mol −1  is needed for hydrogen release. As a result, hydrogen liberation is normally observed at temperatures greater than 300 °C. Although borohydrides are often more thermally stable than alanates, they show quite sluggish reaction kinetics for absorption and desorption of hydrogen. In addition, during the dehydrogenation process, small amounts of volatile boron hydride species may form; these byproducts can affect the hydrogen released by the process, poorly affecting the performance of the fuel cells and reducing the long-term storage capacity of the material [ 8 ].

Amides-Imides  These nitrogen-containing complex hydrides include nitrogen atoms in their chemical network, hence exerting a great influence on both thermodynamic and/or kinetic properties [ 100 ]. The addition of nitrogen increases the structural stability of the hydride, but it also increases the strength of the metal-hydride bond, making the release of hydrogen more energetically costly. Consequently, these materials often require high temperatures and pressures in order to obtain efficient hydrogen absorption and desorption [ 101 ]. Although these materials provide reasonable signs of reversibility when using intermediate hydrogen storage, they nevertheless continue to possess low reaction rates, which continues to be a significant hurdle to their practical use. The research group has been able to show improved performance through various modification schemes such as the addition of catalysts, the creation of nanostructures, and the changing of the compositional nature of materials. The current research efforts for nitrogen-based complex hydrides are aimed at developing a system to achieve higher capacity for hydrogen storage and to maintain thermal stability with rapid hydrogen release [ 102 ].

sections.heading: Elemental hydrides
paragraphs: Elemental hydrides are made directly from one metal element and hydrogen. Magnesium (Mg) is a notable representative of this class.

Mg2Ni is an alloy of magnesium that has great density, very good weight, and the ability to absorb hydrogen in large quantities (6.7%). However, Mg2Ni also has a low amount of heat conductivity and the time required to absorb and release hydrogen is rather high [ 88 ]. Quantitative benchmarking of metal hydrides is shown in Table  5 , which demonstrates the unique benefits and challenges or limitations which exist among the different classes of metal hydrides with respect to their thermodynamics, kinetics, and suitability for real-world applications. While magnesium metal hydrides provide the greatest gravimetric capacity of 7.6 weight percent, the high enthalpy of desorption (70–75 kJ per mole of hydrogen) of magnesium metal hydrides necessitates high temperature conditions for hydrogen release. However, while catalytic modifications and nanostructuring techniques will help to reduce the activation energy for desorption and the temperature required to achieve desorption, thermal management still poses a significant challenge to magnesium metal hydrides. Intermetallic hydrides such as AB5 and AB compounds have excellent hydrogen cycling stability and high hydrogen absorption kinetics and are technologically advanced, contributors to their commercial prevalence. Conversely, the relatively low hydrogen storage capacity of intermetallic hydrides represents a significant limitation for producing relatively high energy density. While complex metal hydrides, such as alanates and borohydrides, theoretically contain very high capacities, their multi-step reaction mechanism and poor reversibility also serve to constrain the available capacity. Novel materials such as high-entropy alloy hydrides and nanoconfined systems are exhibiting promise with respect to tunability and kinetic properties but development has just begun. Consequently, current strategies involving modified magnesium metal hydrides and composite metal hydrides represent the most promising method for developing practical hydrogen storage solutions.

sections.heading: Thermodynamics and kinetics of hydrogen storage
paragraphs: Use of hydrogen as a clean energy source depends on optimizing the thermodynamic/kinetic characteristics of materials used for hydrogen storage [ 110 ]. The current section discusses the underlying fundamental rules that apply to the absorption and desorption of hydrogen with specific reference to the chemical balance between hydride stability and operational working conditions. The thermodynamics dictate the equilibrium that occurs for the storage of hydrogen, and kinetics dictate the rate at which these equilibrium points occur; both parameters are critical for effective storage system development [ 111 ].

sections.heading: Enthalpy and entropy effects on hydrogen storage
paragraphs: The thermodynamic behavior of the systems of metal hydride is dominated primarily by enthalpy and entropy variations for desorption and absorption reactions of hydrogen. The formation of hydrides of metals is an exothermic process with negative enthalpy variations (ΔH) from − 20 kJ/mol(H 2 ) to − 80 kJ/mol(H 2 ), but desorption is an endothermic process, and an input of energy for desorption of hydrogen is needed [ 106 ,  112 ]. This need for energy is a significant challenge for design: highly stable materials with highly negative ΔH can store hydrogen safely but need high temperature for desorption and materials with lower stability with less negative ΔH can desorb at reduced temperatures but might not have sufficient hydrogen storage capacity for atmospheric storage conditions.

The entropic change for hydrogenation is mostly due to the transition from gas molecules of hydrogen to atoms of hydrogen trapped within the lattice of the metal. This process will result in a loss of entropy, which ranges from 110–135 J/mol.K, and which mirrors the diminished translational and rotational freedoms as the gas molecules are trapped inside the solid lattice [ 113 ]. The magnitude of the entropy change will depend upon the structural properties of the host material; highly ordered intermetallic compounds show smaller values of entropy change compared with the complex hydride systems which undergo structural reorganization during hydrogenation [ 113 ].

paragraphs: In Eq. ( 2 ), Peq is the equilibrium plateau pressure, R = the universal gas constant, and T = the absolute temperature [ 114 ]. This equation allows for better determination of which materials to use and how to design systems. If a material is suited for its intended application, this helps to predict the working pressure of a given material at various operational conditions [ 103 ,  115 ,  116 ].

The practical applications of different classes of materials can be demonstrated through material testing, as defined by Van’t Hoff’s equation. The formation enthalpy for LaNi 5  is − 30.6 kJ mol −1 H 2 , and because the equilibrium pressures for LaNi5 at ambient conditions are almost equal to ambient pressure, this means that LaNi5 can also be used at ambient conditions [ 117 ]. The formation enthalpy of MgH 2  is − 75 kJ/mol −1  H 2 ; it needs high pressures (> 350ºC) for hydrogen desorption to have any substantial use commercially until such time as improvements have been made to the hydrogen desorption rate from this material. The data in the table illustrate how the equilibrium pressure and temperature during desorption are correlated to both the formation enthalpy and formation entropy for each material listed. Examples of AB 5 -alloys and TiFe materials are suitable for low-temperature hydrogen storage applications because they have a relatively low desorption enthalpy and operate efficiently at moderate pressures near room temperature, while Mg 2 NiH 4 , NaAlH 4 , and LiBH 4 , which require very high operational temperatures and have significantly higher hydrogen storage capacities because they have high formation enthalpies; structural modifications (alloys modified in the laboratory) also provide the means to achieve improved thermodynamic utility via the use of alloys with a nanostructure.

sections.heading: Pressure-composition-temperature (PCT) relationships
paragraphs: The pressure-composition-temperature (PCT) behavior of metal hydrides provides the most complete thermodynamic description of hydrogen storage in these materials. The PCT analysis shows how hydrogen interacts with the host metal lattice and provides a quantitative measure of the equilibrium conditions for the absorption and desorption of hydrogen, as well as controlling the operational characteristics of any hydride storage system. Hydrogen can be stored in metal hydrides through a reversible solid–gas reaction governed by the Gibbs phase rule and the van’t Hoff equation; thus, PCT diagrams (pressure-composition isotherms, or PCIs) are a vital resource in screening materials, designing reactors, and optimizing systems [ 126 ,  127 ].

To create a Pressure-Composition Isotherm a sample of metal and hydrogen is placed under a defined temperature and its pressure changes as more or less hydrogen is added to the sample. An example of this graph is in Fig.  8 a. The PCI graph has three regions that represent the phases present in a metal-hydrogen sample. Figure 8 a  The Pressure Composition Isotherm (PCT) curve and Van’t Hoff curves of metal-based alloys and complex hydrides.  b  Schematic showing the energy barriers to the hydrogenation process of metal-based alloys and complex hydrides. Reprinted from [ 128 ], with permission from John Wiley & Sons.

1. α-phase (Solid Solution Region)  At very low levels of hydrogen, interstitial hydrogen atoms will dissolve into the metallic lattice without forming any new phase; this is known as the α phase (solid solution) as is indicated by the steep rise in pressure with increased hydrogen concentration because of the random location of the dissolved atoms in interstitial sites. For most metals, the solubility limit is generally low (< 0.1–0.5 H/M atomic ratio) and conforms with Sieverts’ law (square root of concentration with respect to pressure). Although this phase has little practical use for storage purposes, it aids in our understanding of initial activation and the kinetics of surface processes [ 129 ].

2. Plateau Region (Two-Phase Coexistence: α  +  β)  A new hydride phase (β-phase) forms when the solubility limit of the α-phase is reached. At that point two phases (α & β) coexist in equilibrium. According to Gibbs’ phase rule, the equilibrium pressure of the system remains constant while the overall composition changes from an α-phase to a β-phase at constant temperature. This explains the characteristic flat plateau seen in metal hydride systems. The plateau pressure (P_eq) is the most important design characteristic for metal hydride materials. Metal hydrides with P_eq values between 1 and 10 bar at moderate temperatures (0 °C–100 °C) will provide a good balance of hydrogen storage capacity, safe operation, and energy efficiency. The length of the plateau will directly determine the reversibility of hydrogen uptake by the metal hydride material, i.e., how much hydrogen can be absorbed/released in a practical (realistic operating) manner [ 130 ].

3. β-phase (Hydride Region)  Once the plateau has been reached, adding more hydrogen will yield more Beta-hydride; however, the pressure will increase steeply due to the hydrogen having to enter into an already full lattice. Hence, this configuration is typically not suitable for reversible storage due to the extremely high pressures required [ 131 ].

As PCIs are evaluated across different temperatures (T1 < T2 < T3), the isotherm lines rise up as you go to higher temperatures. The pressure on the plateaus is higher for H 2  because desorption is endothermic & higher temperatures result in the release of more H 2  from the material. The natural logarithm of the plateau pressure (ln Peq) vs 1/T produces the van’t Hoff diagram, shown in Fig.  8 b, with slope = − ΔH/R & the y intercept = ΔS/R (where ΔH is the enthalpy of hydride formation, typically − 20 to − 80 kJ mol −1  H 2 , & R is the gas constant; ΔS is primarily from the loss of translational entropy of the H 2  gas (typically − 110 to − 135 J mol −1  K −1 ). The two thermodynamic properties described provide the basis for accurate operating temperatures and pressures for all hydride forms [ 27 ].
In ideal materials, the plateau would be completely flat and demonstrate consistent phase transformations throughout the material. In practice, however, the following is often observed:

Plateau slope  These deviations can be attributed to a variety of reasons, including compositional inhomogeneity, variation in particle size distributions, or lattice strain. A slope across the plateau gives a lower usable reversible capacity, as some of the hydrogen is only released at pressures outside the desired operating range [ 132 ].

Hysteresis  The pressure at the absorption plateau is always greater than the pressure at the desorption plateau. This is due to the differences in interfacial energy, elastic strain energy and plastic deformation, as can be seen in Fig.  9 , between the absorption and desorption processes. When hysteresis occurs, energy loss occurs on each cycle, which results in a reduction in the usable pressure range [ 133 ]. Figure 9 Schematic representation of absorption (solid) and desorption (dashed) processes in the PCT curve. Reprinted from [ 27 ], with permission from Elsevier.

Non-ideal behaviors limit reversible hydrogen capacity and make managing temperature and mechanical issues more difficult. In a vehicle application, using a sloped or hysteretic plateau may result in larger temperature differences or greater pressures, thus increasing the complexity and cost of the system. In terms of stationary storage, hysteresis leads to reduced round-trip efficiency due to the need for additional heat/work being applied to fill the pressure gap [ 134 ].

The PCT technique is not simply for diagnosis, but also predicts future performance. By analyzing the same set of isotherms, an engineer can determine exactly what temperature/pressure will result in the desired amount of material stored; engineers can then design heat exchangers to properly manage the reaction enthalpy and select appropriate materials for use during a given range of operation (e.g., electrolyzers or fuel cells). Using high-throughput methods combined with machine-learning-based analyses, today’s PCT instrumentation allows for very rapid screening of hundreds of compositions and, therefore, helps to expedite the identification of promising new hydrides that exhibit flatter plateaus, lower hysteresis, and tunable thermodynamic properties [ 134 ].

To summarize, the PCT plot along with the van’t Hoff plot form the basis of thermodynamics for metal hydrides for hydrogen storage applications. The microscopic phenomena related to phase change are converted into macroscopic engineering parameters such as plateau pressure, capacity, temperature, and enthalpy. The deviation from the ideal plateau is one of the key issues in the design and development of hydrogen storage materials.

sections.heading: Kinetics of hydrogen storage
paragraphs: The energy required to start the process of hydrogen adsorption/desorption is what dictates the kinetics of the hydrogen storage materials. Certain ranges of cycling parameters (temperature, time) to achieve efficient hydrogen storage will depend upon the known values of activation energies associated with a variety of hydrogen storage materials and processes between 50 − 200 kJ/ mol  −1  [ 135 ]. For example, pure MgH 2  requires higher temperatures and longer processing times to achieve the optimum rate of hydrogen desorption because the activation energy for desorption is high (181.4 kJ mol) [ 136 ]. Figure  10  depicts the interactions that occur between thermodynamic and kinetic forces governing these reactions. The figure also illustrates how some combination or other of the thermodynamic parameters (enthalpy change, equilibrium pressure, and desorption temperature) and kinetic parameters (activation energy, hydrogen diffusion, and desorption rate) will affect the storage capacity of Mg-based alloys. The figure shows that a delicate balance must be achieved in order for maximum performance to be realized from hydrogen storage [ 137 ]. Figure 10 Correlation between the thermodynamic and kinetic properties of hydriding and dehydriding reactions in Mg-based alloys and their hydrogen storage behavior. Reprinted from [ 138 ], with permission from elsevier.

Hydrogen storage involves a group of unique steps involving particular activation energies. These steps are: (1) hydrogen adsorption onto the solid surface; (2) dissociation of hydrogen molecules; (3) diffusion of hydrogen atoms through the solid matrix; (4) phase nucleation of the metal hydride; (5) growth of the metal hydride phase; and (6) migration of the phase boundaries. The rate-limiting step will be specific to each solid material, temperature, and processing condition, thus requiring a tailored optimization approach for all of these to enhance their respective kinetics [ 111 ,  135 ].

sections.heading: Catalytic effects and enhancement strategies
paragraphs:
Economically, using catalyst elements for kinetic rate enhancement is the most optimal solution. Historically, transition metal elements (i.e., Nb, Ni, and Ti) have been extremely useful for optimizing activation energies and increasing the rate of hydrogen absorption/desorption in their associated processes. Multiple mechanisms are involved in the way catalysts work, such as accelerating the dissociation of hydrogen molecules at surfaces, giving additional diffusion routes across the material, and forming beneficial nucleation sites for phase changes [ 139 ]. A more detailed mechanistic discussion of how catalyst doping and nano-sizing modify hydrogen sorption in MgH₂-based systems is provided in Sect. " Mechanisms of Enhancement ". The effectiveness of different catalytic systems in improving the hydrogen desorption performance of MgH 2 -based materials is summarized in Table  7 .

sections.heading: Synthesis optimization methods
paragraphs: Ball milling of materials, decreasing the particle dimensions, increasing the surface area, adding structural imperfections, and allowing close catalyst mixing, has been characterized as an effective technique for enhancing the kinetics of hydrogen storage. Increasing ball milling time systematically increases the kinetics of the process by creating new surfaces, forming lattice imperfections that facilitate the diffusion of hydrogen, and achieving catalyst distribution in the material matrix [ 148 ]. Ball milling efficiency depends on milling time, energy input, and atmospheric conditions; ball milling in a hydrogen atmosphere using high energy allows the simultaneous formation of hydrides and their structural modification as confirmed in mechano-chemical fabrication routes producing nanocrystalline hydrides with enhanced kinetic parameters. Ball milling MgH 2  for 20 h reduces its activation energy by ~ 85.2 kJ/mol, while maintaining its structural integrity and storage capacity [ 110 ,  111 ]. Other synthesis methods for optimizing kinetics, which include melt spinning and chemical doping, achieve results through different mechanisms because melt spinning creates rapidly solidified alloys that possess nanocrystalline microstructures that contain evenly distributed catalysts, and chemical doping introduces fillers, which they apply in specific patterns to modify electronic configurations and phase stability. Mechanically prepared high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have superior kinetics; specific systems such as TiVZrNbNi exhibiting as low as 65.4 kJ/mol, with desorption temperatures around 180 °C [ 149 ].

sections.heading: Intermetallic hydrides
paragraphs: AB 5 -type intermetallics (such as LaNi 5 ) have − 25 to − 35 kJ/mol formation enthalpies and 20–80 °C working temperature ranges. The materials have favorable kinetics with minimal activation energies and good H cycling performance, so can be used for near-ambient applications. But, due to their gravimetric store levels of 1.3–1.4 wt%, they do not perform very well within applications where weight sensitivity is a significant factor [ 150 ]. AB 2  Laves phase-based alloys have an intermediate AB 5  compound and high-capacity material properties. They have formation enthalpies ranging from − 28.0 kJ/mol(H 2 ) with desorption temperatures of 50 °C and have a good balance between stability and working conditions. Compositional variation and catalyst addition for the enhancement of kinetics allow for practical cycling rates of H 2  with reasonable storage capacities [ 27 ].

sections.heading: Complex hydrides and light metal hydrides
paragraphs: NaAlH 4  has a formation enthalpy of − 37.0 kJ/mol, requiring desorption temperatures up to 180 °C, and LiBH 4  has a formation enthalpy of − 75.0 kJ/mol, requiring desorption temperatures over 380 °C [ 135 ]. These complex hybrids have high theoretical H 2  storage capacities, but the thermodynamic/kinetic barriers originate from strong bonding with hydrogen and from the complicated anion structure. MgH 2,  with a high theoretical capacity (7.6%) and an available low-cost feedstock, is a promising material. However, its high formation enthalpy of − 75.0 kJ/mol and high activation energy barrier (> 180 kJ/mol) counter its practical benefits [ 151 ]. Researchers have conducted extensive studies to develop catalyst development methods and synthesis procedures that can overcome existing system limitations. The most recent doping techniques for MgH 2  have produced remarkable improvements in rate kinetics. The system efficiency has been enhanced through enhancements to both the catalytic system and its corresponding processing methods. The multi-compositional catalysts in these methods enable activation energy reduction beyond 50% while achieving desorption temperature limits [ 146 ]. The different catalytic mechanisms work together to enhance multiple hydrogen storage process elements.

sections.heading: Magnesium-based hydrides: high capacity, enhanced by nano-sizing and catalyst doping
paragraphs: Among lightweight metal hydrides, magnesium hydride (MgH 2 ) is widely considered to be one of the most promising solid-state hydrogen storage mediums with a gravimetric capacity of over 7.6 percent hydrogen, a relatively low material cost, and a virtually unrestricted supply. However, implementing MgH 2  in practice is hampered by high temperatures that are necessary to drive hydrogen desorption and the slowness of kinetics, due to which the period of hydrogen extraction into the lattice is significantly increased. These two inherent shortcomings make the use of MgH 2  and associated metal hydrides largely inapplicable to the real-life implementation of hydrogen storage solutions. The latest studies have been geared toward designing structural changes and additives that accomplish catalysis, and the goal here is to optimally raise the hydrogen liberation rate and also lower the temperature at which the material is to operate, synergistically [ 152 ].

Table  8  gives an account of the comparative analysis of different modifications carried out on MgH2 to show the effect of particle size and catalyst addition on hydrogen desorption temperatures and capacities. The research demonstrates that nano-sized MgH 2  materials release hydrogen at lower temperatures, which range from 119 to 281 °C, while maintaining their hydrogen storage capacity of approximately 7.6 weight percent. The reaction kinetics of catalyst-doped systems, which include Nb 2 O 5  and Ti-CoO@C and Mn and Ni/MnO-modified MgH 2 , demonstrate improved performance through reduced activation energy requirements and enhanced cycling stability, which enables faster and reversible hydrogen uptake and release.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of enhancement
paragraphs: Nano-Sizing  Reducing the size of MgH 2  to nano-levels increases the rate of hydrogen uptake because of the reduced diffusion distance and the modification of the transport mechanism. Reduced diffusion distances mean faster rates of both absorption and release of hydrogen. The high number of grain boundaries, dislocations, vacancies, and phase boundaries on nanosized deformed Mg/MgH 2  creates pathways for fast diffusion and provides nucleation sites for fast nucleation and movement of phase boundaries. The effect of surface and interface energies on free energy is higher at the nanometer scale and tends to destabilize MgH 2  thermodynamically, thus reducing the enthalpy of dehydrogenation and the required desorption temperature compared to bulk MgH 2 . Nano-MgH 2  starts to release hydrogen at 119 °C, which is lower than the 280 °C release temperature of the bulk material. The structural benefits of the system work together to speed up reaction processes while improving the ability to reversibly store hydrogen, which Table  8  shows [ 153 ,  155 ,  160 ,  161 ,  162 – 163 ].

Catalyst Doping  The role of catalyst doping in improving the hydrogen sorption properties of MgH2 is associated with changes in reaction processes at interfaces, not merely its introduction. The process starts with adsorption of H 2  molecules onto the catalyst-coated surface, followed by their easy dissociation because of the decreased activation energy for dissociation caused by the catalyst. Further, atomic hydrogen moves through the catalyst/Mg or catalyst/MgH 2  interface into the matrix due to enhanced diffusion. Interfaces and catalysts also provide conditions for nucleation that reduce the energy barriers for hydride formation in absorption and desorption processes. Finally, these sites facilitate recombination and desorption processes upon release. It can be noted that in accordance with the Sabatier principle, low affinity between hydrogen atoms and catalysts reduces hydrogen adsorption/dissociation, whereas high affinity prevents its diffusion/recombination. Therefore, catalysts with optimal H 2  adsorption energies are more favorable for all reactions listed above. Effective catalysts include transition metals and oxides (Ti, Nb, Ni, Mn, Zr-containing). Adding catalysts, like Nb 2 O 5 , Ti-based composites, or Mn-based additives, has been shown to decrease desorption temperatures by 60–140 °C and to increase both hydrogen release and uptake rates significantly [ 125 ,  158 ,  159 ,  164 ,  165 ,  166 ,  167 – 168 ].

Table  9  and Fig.  11  illustrate the role of nano-sizing and catalyst doping in hydrogen storage using MgH 2 . Nano-sizing increases the surface area and facilitates diffusion through grain boundaries and also destabilizes the system thermodynamically to some extent, whereas catalyst doping helps only in dissociating H 2  and facilitating hydrogen transfer.

sections.heading: Synergistic effects and future directions
paragraphs: One can achieve the synergistic effect of faster kinetics and improved cyclability of MgH 2  as a real hydrogen storage material by combining nano-sizing with multi-catalyst systems (e.g., transition metals plus metal oxides or carbon materials), which in turn has been confirmed by several independent studies [ 67 ,  153 ,  155 ,  159 ,  169 ,  170 ]. The goal of the present research is to find the best combination of catalyst types, distribution, and nanostructuring methods to lower the operating temperature and further increase the reversibility.

Through nano-sizing and catalyst doping, magnesium-based hydrides have been radically reformulated from a material with very high capacity but impractical operating conditions into materials with great potential for use as a hydrogen storage medium, featuring a significant reduction in operating temperature and an improvement in kinetics. On the road to the first commercial application, research work in the above-mentioned areas undoubtedly will lead to further development of MgH 2 -based systems.

sections.heading: Hydrogen storage using high-entropy alloys (HEAs): adaptable compositions and enhancement in performance
paragraphs: High‐Entropy Alloys (HEAs) are emerging as highly promising materials for hydrogen storage due to their rich compositional design space and unique structural features. By combining multiple principal elements (often in near‐equiatomic proportions), HEAs can form solid‐solution or Laves‐phase structures with high configurational entropy, lattice distortion, and multivalent electronic states. These features enable them to offer numerous, different interstitial sites, facilitate hydrogen diffusion, and improve thermodynamic and kinetic behavior. For example, the TiCrMnFeZr HEA incorporated into MgH 2  (≈ 40 wt%) markedly improves desorption onset to ≈ 162 °C, compared to much higher temperatures in pure MgH 2 , and allows ~ 3.7 wt% H 2  release at 230 °C within 60 min, with excellent cycling stability [ 171 ]. The equiatomic HEA catalysts TiVNbZrFe reduce the desorption temperature of MgH 2  by approximately 170 °C while they maintain their ability to release about 6.16 wt% of hydrogen through multiple tests [ 171 ]. Zr-based HEAs with Mg substitution have been shown to absorb some 0.8 to 0.9 wt.% H 2  at ambient temperature, far easier than corresponding non-Mg HEAs when they undergo such substitution because of their lower electron concentration and better lattice distortion [ 172 ]. The examples presented indicate that HEAs may be used under lower temperatures, and, thus, enhance cycling performance, or maintain or further develop it by accelerating hydrogen uptake. Such materials allow systematically modulating the strength of hydrogen binding as well as phase architecture and defect landscapes, thus providing an effective methodology of developing hydrogen-storage materials with high performance.

sections.heading: Design principles and critical considerations in HEA-based hydrogen storage
paragraphs: While the performance of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), particularly for hydrogen storage applications, is promising, it has not been established as an unpredictable phenomenon. This has created a need to investigate the link between the chemical composition of an HEA and its properties, such as thermodynamic stability, electron configuration, and crystal structure/parameters [ 173 ,  174 ].

sections.heading: Thermodynamic tuning via element selection
paragraphs: The hydrogen uptake/desorption properties of HEAs depend greatly on the hydride formation enthalpy (ΔH), which must be within the right range (~ 20—50 kJ/mol H₂) in order for reversible hydrogen storage to occur under realistic conditions [ 175 ]. Metals including titanium (Ti), vanadium (V), and zirconium (Zr) have the ability to form stable hydrides because of their high affinity to hydrogen. In contrast, metals including iron (Fe), chromium (Cr), and nickel (Ni) make it more difficult for hydrides to be stabilized, thereby lowering the desorption temperature of hydrogen. Thus, compositions such as TiVNbZrFe achieve a balanced thermodynamic profile, where strong hydride-forming elements are moderated by weaker ones, enabling reversible hydrogen release at reduced temperatures [ 176 ,  177 ].

sections.heading: Role of lattice distortion and configurational entropy
paragraphs: The essential characteristic of an HEA is that it has extreme lattice distortion due to the variability between the sizes of atoms that make up each element of the alloy [ 178 ]. Through these dimensions and the resulting lattice distortion, many different interstitial sites can form for the accommodation of hydrogen. Due to the distortion of the lattice of Platinum-Group metals such as TiCrMnFeZr, hydrogen can diffuse through the metals more quickly, meaning that these alloys will have lower energy barriers for diffusion and faster hydrogen absorption kinetics [ 169 ].

sections.heading: Valence electron concentration (VEC) and phase stability
paragraphs: The valence electron concentration (VEC) is a critical parameter in determining the phase formation in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), where lower VEC values (< ~ 6.8) favor the formation of BCC structures, which are beneficial for hydrogen storage, while higher VEC values (> ~ 8) stabilize FCC phases that are less favorable due to their limited interstitial space [ 174 ]. Consequently, BCC-dominant systems such as TiVZrNbNi exhibit higher hydrogen diffusivity, greater storage capacity, and improved absorption/desorption kinetics [ 179 ]. An example of this is when phase coexistence (BCC and Laves phases) also creates a heterogeneous distribution of hydrogen that makes the hydrogen reversible.

sections.heading: Electronic structure and hydrogen binding
paragraphs: The electronic structure governs hydrogen interaction with high-entropy alloys primarily through d-band filling and electron distribution, where early transition metals such as Ti, V, and Nb enhance hydrogen chemisorption, while late transition metals such as Ni and Fe modify binding energy and facilitate catalytic dissociation. This demonstrates that multi-principal compositions outperform binary alloys by simultaneously optimizing the key processes of hydrogen adsorption, dissociation, and diffusion.

sections.heading: Synergistic catalytic effects
paragraphs: Some HEAs function not only as hydrogen storage media but also as catalysts in MgH₂ systems, where they reduce activation energy (as observed in TiVZrNbNi systems), enhance hydrogen dissociation kinetics, and improve cycling stability due to their uniform elemental distribution. This multifunctionality represents a significant advantage of HEAs over traditional intermetallic hydrides.

sections.heading: Composition-tunability and structural features
paragraphs: High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) are mixtures of 5 or more primary chemical elements combined in nearly equal proportions. Their solid-solution phases are characterized by either body-centered cubic (BCC) or face-centered cubic (FCC) structures due in part to high configurational entropy. Their usefulness in hydrogen storage applications is contingent upon the alloys’ design to provide the ideal atomic-scale configurations for optimum hydrogen affinity, thermodynamic stability, and microstructural features to facilitate maximum hydrogen absorption. The multi-phase structures of HEAs create conditions that allow for hydrogen absorption. The structural characteristics of HEAs can be engineered, creating new and unique alloys with the ability to provide multiple phases with the appropriate thermodynamic properties. Therefore, HEAs contain an abundance of accessible configurational states, resulting in multiple potential sites for hydrogen absorption on a sub-micrometer scale.

sections.heading: Hydrogen storage performance
paragraphs: HEAs therefore have a unique combination of advantageous features that promise to provide exceptional hydrogen-storage mating materials. They are composed primarily of 5 or more primary elements, which form part of both stable and unstable solids. In addition, the configuration of the HEAs can be designed and created in a manner that allows for the presence of a pure solid solution, as observed in some cases where the HEA has only been formed as a simple cubic, body-centered cubic and face-centered cubic solid-solution, as well as those that have formed as more complex multi-phase alloy structures. Thus, the HEA may represent an exciting avenue for innovative hydrogen-storage development.

Hydrogen Storage Capacity  There is a wide range of hydrogen storage capabilities for high-entropy alloys, ranging from 1.6 to 3.6wt%, depending on the composition of the elements and on the way in which they are made. The alloy chemistry that includes TiVZrNbHf has also achieved an H/M ratio of nearly 2.5, which provides performance that is very similar to that of many conventional intermetallics and metal hydride systems [ 87 ,  147 ,  180 ,  181 – 182 ]. The increased storage capability results from the multiple synergistic effects that improve stability of the hydrogen phase as well as provide the ability for the hydrogen atom to be accommodated into the lattice through an expansion of the lattice. The compositional flexibility of HEAs makes it possible to fine-tune the hydrogen affinity and the binding energy, thus making it possible to harness reversible storage operation and scalability.

Kinetics and Reversibility  Hydrogen absorption and desorption on the high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are usually fast and highly reversible, which makes these materials interesting in practice. The activation enthalpies of most HEAs are low, and they are highly cyclically stable, despite innumerable hydrogenation steps and dehydrogenation cycles. More specifically, it is proven possible to produce special alloy systems, which enable such materials to absorb hydrogen (at or close to ambient temperature) without the materials undergoing any preceding pre-activating cycles [ 87 ,  166 ,  183 ]. More specifically, it is proven possible to produce special alloy systems, which enable such materials to absorb hydrogen (at or close to ambient temperature) without the materials undergoing any preceding pre-activating cycles [ 184 ]. Such alloys are characterized by highly disordered lattice structures and high defect densities, which promote strong effective hydrogen diffusion tracks. In addition, the uniformity of the constituent elements in the solid solution increases the flexibility of the lattice, hence reducing the strain concentration under successive cycles, and increasing reversibility.

Phase Structure and Microstructural Influence  Hydrogen storage features of HEAs rely on the phase structure and microstructure. Hydrogen diffusivity and storage capacities are enhanced in alloys that contain body-centered cubic (BCC) structures and Laves phases. The atomic structures of such phases form an open structure that provides numerous interstitial sites that allow swift diffusion of hydrogen [ 182 ,  185 ,  186 ]. Performance phase design shows compositional modulation and thermal processing success. The secondary or multiple phases provide more diffusion avenues through the interface and, in so doing, enhance the hydrogen kinetics. The microstructural control is the most influential aspect of hydrogen-storage HEA developments.

Challenges and Future Prospects  Notable advancements have been made in hydrogen storage technology, though there remain significant challenges to improvements in HA-based hydrogen storage material. Most notable improvements require clarification regarding atomic structure in relation to material functioning and the thermodynamic response, while also requiring larger sample volumes with more weight capacity. The development trajectory is directly controlled by machine-learning method integration and thermodynamic models, allowing researchers to predict steady material compositional and hydrogen-absorption profiles. They provide a platform for designing new HEAs with enhanced storage capacity while minimizing the need for large-scale experimental studies [ 187 ,  188 – 189 ].

HEAs show outstanding potential as hydrogen storage materials for future generations, as the storage capacity can be reversed, and their storage speed can be adjusted by making the necessary compositional changes. This makes them be considered as worthy candidates to be incorporated into practical hydrogen energy systems. Current and future research efforts focus on two main goals, which include improving hydrogen storage capabilities and developing industrial-scale synthesis methods and studying the essential mechanisms behind their unique hydrogen–metal interactions.

sections.heading: Hydride composites with MOFs and graphene
paragraphs: Initial studies have shown that the two types of hydrogen storage materials (hydride composites) have superior thermal conductivity and hydrogen diffusion than either type can provide on its own. This suggests that using both MOFs and graphene-based materials for hydrogen storage could provide greater benefit than using either type of material independently.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of enhancement
paragraphs: Graphene and Graphene Oxide (GO)  Due to its large surface area, good mechanical properties, and high thermal conductivity, the presence of graphene facilitates the dispersion of the hydride materials, reduces agglomeration of hydride particles, ensures uniform distribution of heat through the body of the hydride, and provides a medium for transporting hydrogen. This results in higher cycle stability and an increased rate of hydrogen transport through absorption and desorption [ 26 ,  190 ,  191 – 192 ]. MOFs  MOFs offer a porous substrate with a highly specialized surface area for H 2  storage, as well as an adjustable pore diameter which allows for nanoscale confinement of hydrides; therefore, the temperature of H 2  release may be lowered and reversibility can be improved.

The role of advanced materials in hydrogen storage is illustrated in Tables  10  and  11 . While Table  10  shows graphene/MOF composites that offer kinetic improvements as well as heat control with higher hydrogen uptake capabilities, Table  11  highlights various other material categories, focusing on tuning thermodynamics, catalysis, and storage improvements.

Synergistic Effects  Using graphene or graphene-based products as a supplement to MOFs has resulted in increased quantities of active sites, total pore volume, and surface area of both materials, thereby improving the kinetic reaction rate and capacity of both materials to store H 2 .

Thermal Conductivity  The high thermal conductivity of graphene facilitates the transfer of heat that occurs during H 2  adsorption/desorption, thereby reducing the temperature gradient, making the system more reliable.

Hydrogen Spillover  In addition to metal catalysts (e.g., Pt, Ni), metal organic framework (MOF) / graphene composites may also provide a means of enhancing H 2  storage capacity through “spillover” mechanisms.

Optimization  The maximum efficiency of several systems is dependent upon three important variables: selection of a metal–organic framework (MOF), modification of the surface of graphene, and modification of the composite structure.

MOF-modified graphene/hydride composites, as described in Table  7 , resulted in increased thermal conductivity and hydrogen diffusion, which produced faster chemical reactions, increased the capacity for storing hydrogen and provided a more stable cycle. These advancements are touted as the beginning of a new generation of environmentally-friendly hydrogen storage technology.

sections.heading: Additive manufacturing & thin films: structured hydrogen storage devices with built-in heat management
paragraphs: Thin film technologies and additive manufacturing open up new horizons of hydrogen storage devices’ development by offering unorthodox ways of doing things beyond the conventional design practices. This is just one of many advantages that include controlling matter, composition, and thermal properties at the level of a single atomic layer. The methods help developers to build products that store hydrogen more efficiently and maintain better heat control in their designs. The LMD, SLM, and EBM additive manufacturing technologies allow for the production of different microstructures by mixing various alloys and hydride materials. These techniques provide:

Design Freedom  Design freedom is possible in 3D printing technology through AM, which can produce porous and layered intricate structural designs to enhance hydrogen flow and thermal regulation in storage units, respectively. Designers of lattice-structured metal hydride reactors and flow-field plates in Fig.  12 a–b can design systems to inherently maintain hydrogen distribution by design and meet mechanical strength requirements through surface area increase. Figure 12 Examples of additively manufactured hydrogen components:  a  metal hydride reactor;  b  stainless steel flow-field plates;  c  conductive/non-conductive PLA bipolar plates;  d  copper-based spiral electrode;  e  porous SiC catalyst supports;  f  printed gas diffusion layer for a PEM fuel cell. Reproduced from [ 6 ] under a CC BY license.

Rapid Solidification  Rapid Solidification arising from melting and ultra-fast cooling rates is responsible for localized melting in LMD, SLM, and EBM processes. This results in crystallographic patterns with a reduced grain size and reduced crystallographic damage. The refinement culminates in the production of AM-derived components with enhanced hydrogen sorption kinetics, mechanical integrity, and improved fatigue resistance over repeated hydrogen cycling. Copper-based electrodes and SiC catalytic supports shown in Fig.  12 d–e demonstrate that microstructural refinement increases reaction rates and thermal conductivity.

Material Homogeneity  3D printing through in-situ alloying ensures the homogeneity of elements in materials and prevents phase-segregation within materials during the AM process. Hydrides and alloys of a chemically consistent composition can be produced through this process, assuring consistent hydrogen storage capacity and giving the alloys a great amount of durability over a lengthy duration of operation. The hydrides and alloys created through this process will be 3D printed, exhibiting a homogeneous chemical composition, and will provide the same hydrogen storage capacity as well as durability after a lengthy period of usage [ 187 ].

sections.heading: Thin film deposition technologies: layered architectures for efficient hydrogen storage and thermal regulation
paragraphs: Hydrogen storage technologies that use these techniques have been developed using advanced thin film deposition methods (such as sputtering, ALD, and dip coating) to create hydrogen storage materials with designed interfaces and nanostructured growth patterns, along with intrinsic temperature control mechanisms. These approaches enable the fabrication of materials on an atomic scale using thin films (of specific thickness) with specific chemical compositions and morphologies, resulting in materials having superior hydrogen kinetic performance and controlled heat transfer capabilities.

Enabled Surface Area  Fabricating thin films drastically increases the surface-to-volume ratio. Thus hydrogen will be able to have contact with active sites faster, and the diffusion length in the hydride phase will be shortened. Additionally, ALD and sputter-deposited films exhibit excellent control of film thickness, uniformity, and surface texture, which provide rapid hydrogen absorption/desorption cycles. The morphology of these films makes them suitable for the micro/nano-scale energy devices in which hydrogen needs to be reactive and have a short diffusion path to allow for efficient operation. For example, a reversible hydrogen storage MoO film manufactured via ALD has been found to provide volumetric hydrogen storage equivalent to pressurized gas cylinders while maintaining its thin-film morphology [ 204 ,  205 ,  206 – 207 ].

Layered Structures  Layered structures (e.g., Mg/Ti/Ni; Mg/Fe; Pd/Mg/Pd) create constrained diffusion paths, localized heat channels, and assist in the structural integrity of the material during hydrogen release. The metal hydride layer interfaces work as thermal bridges; thus, heat dissipation is improved and desorption temperatures can be lowered by more than 100 C in comparison with bulk MgH 2 . These aspects are in agreement with Table  8 , which indicates that multilayer films have superior hydrogen kinetics and efficient heat flow. NiMgNiMg multilayer films fabricated by magnetron sputtering have exhibited reversible hydrogen content exceeding 4 wt.% at ambient pressure due to interface effects and structural confinement [ 208 ,  209 ,  210 – 211 ].

Integrated Sensing and Control  Thin films can be designed to detect and control hydrogen in real time through integrated sensing and control. By integrating sensing elements or optoelectronic layers within the film, it is possible to monitor hydrogen concentration and thermal conditions during operation. Such self-regulating coatings improve safety and efficiency in hydrogen systems, especially in compact or mobile energy devices. For example, ultrathin TiO 2  coatings made by ALD stabilize AlH 3  particles and are catalytically active in controlling hydrogen kinetics [ 212 ,  213 ,  214 – 215 ].

Engineers can create structured hydrogen storage materials with integrated heat management and the desired high-rate hydrogen kinetics by combining thin film technologies with innovative manufacturing techniques. This is paving the way for the creation of energy systems that use hydrogen that are not only safer and more effective but also scalable in size.
