sections.heading: Artificial intelligence and machine learning for hydride discovery
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly transforming the discovery and optimization of hydrogen storage materials, particularly metal hydrides. As opposed to traditional methods of experimentation, ML allows for a fast way to explore large compositional as well as structural design spaces, by learning the complicated relationships between descriptors of materials and their hydrogen storage behavior. In addition, recent research has shown that using an ML-driven framework can greatly reduce the cost of experimentation and accelerate the discovery of good-performing hydrides [ 83 ,  216 ,  217 ].

sections.heading: Training datasets and data sources
paragraphs: The quality and variety of training data have a significant influence on the prediction power of machine learning models. The datasets used for hydrogen storage research will typically be built from three types of data sources, which include: Data derived from Density Functional Theory (DFT) databases (e.g., Materials Project and OQMD). These databases provide information (e.g., formation energy, hydrogen binding energy, electronic structure) about each material's hydrogen storage potential. Experimental datasets were used to create PCT data, thermodynamic properties, and kinetic measurements. High-throughput datasets (e.g., generated by the combinatorial screening of the hydrogen storage characteristics of a vast number of hydrides) provide detailed information about hydrogen storage capability.

As an example, Verma et al. utilized more than 14,000 experimental data points across 138 different hydrides to develop a significant dataset for the purpose of enabling predictions of PCT behavior through ML. Also, supervised ML models trained on datasets provided by the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) have produced successful predictions of hydrogen storage capacity based on different thermodynamic conditions. Nonetheless, the lack of standardized or high-quality experimental datasets continues to create a significant barrier to the development of reliable predictive ML models [ 218 ].

sections.heading: Feature selection and descriptor engineering
paragraphs: Feature engineering plays a critical role in determining model accuracy, with commonly used descriptors including compositional features such as atomic radius, electronegativity, and valence electron concentration; thermodynamic parameters such as enthalpy (ΔH), entropy (ΔS), and equilibrium pressure; structural descriptors including lattice constants, crystal symmetry, and interstitial site size; and electronic features such as density of states and band structure characteristics. Advanced feature selection techniques, including principal component analysis (PCA), recursive feature elimination (RFE), and SHAP analysis, have been widely applied to identify the most influential variables governing hydrogen absorption and desorption behavior. For example, Maghsoudy et al. demonstrated that a reduced set of 22 optimized descriptors could achieve prediction accuracy with  R 2  values close to 0.98 for AB₂-type hydrides [ 219 ].

sections.heading: Machine learning models and validation strategies

Various machine learning algorithms have been employed to model hydrogen storage properties, including Random Forest (RF) and Gradient Boosting for nonlinear regression, Support Vector Machines (SVM) for the classification of stable hydrides, and Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) for capturing complex structure–property relationships. Model validation is essential to ensure reliability and generalization, with common strategies including k-fold cross-validation to minimize overfitting, the use of performance metrics such as root mean square error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), and coefficient of determination ( R 2 ), as well as external validation datasets to evaluate model transferability (Table  13 ).

sections.heading: Case Studies of AI-guided hydride discovery
paragraphs: The following paper examples provide evidence that ML-assisted material discovery has proven successful in practice: High-throughput ML (machine learning) screening of Magnesium-based hydrides has evaluated over 600 different combinations of Mg-based (hydride) chemistry, providing over 30 candidates (hydrides) with better hydrogen storage properties [ 233 ]. ML was also successfully used for high-throughput screening of all Mg-based alloys for hydrogen storage and energy conversion. ML-assisted optimization of MgH₂ systems has identified the best available dopants for the reduction of the hydrogen desorption temperature while maintaining a high storage capacity for MgH₂[ 233 ]. The exploration of ternary alloy hydrides and high-entropy alloy hydrides via database (data-driven) approaches has projected combinations of compositions having greater hydrogen diffusivity and better reversibility[ 176 ]. Models developed utilizing neural networks trained on extensive datasets have produced accurate predictions of new borohydrides that possess optimum thermodynamic characteristics for more efficient hydrogen release at lower temperatures [ 234 ].

The above-stated case studies provide evidence that ML-assisted methods are good practices to help researchers develop materials faster by reducing the number of materials developed based on error-prone trial-and-error approaches.

sections.heading: Limitations and challenges
paragraphs: Despite considerable advancements, several challenges remain, including data scarcity, where the lack of reliable experimental datasets limits model robustness; limited model interpretability, as complex approaches such as deep neural networks do not provide clear physical insights into their functioning; transferability issues, where models developed for one type of hydride may not generalize well across different hydride systems; and dataset bias, where the overrepresentation of well-studied materials such as MgH₂ and LaNi₅ hinders the discovery of new candidates. Beltrame et al. further indicated that machine learning models suffer from limited generalizability due to insufficient data diversity [ 218 ], highlighting the need for improved dataset coverage, along with the development of explainable and interpretable AI frameworks for materials science applications [ 235 ].

sections.heading: Challenges in the application of metal hydrides in real life
paragraphs: Despite the remarkable potential of metal hydrides for hydrogen storage, their real-world application is hindered by several interconnected challenges, as illustrated in Fig.  14 . To achieve high efficiency, it is necessary to have materials with very large surface areas and porosities that can promote hydrogen diffusion and kinetics; at the same time, such materials should be capable of withstanding the strain effects of repeated cycling. In addition, the improvement of the catalytic activity as well as the electrical or thermal conductivity is necessary for the quick absorption/desorption and good heat management. Unfortunately, these enhancements can lead to more complex processing and higher costs. Designing materials that can store a large amount of hydrogen while keeping the weight and size of the whole system to a minimum is a difficult task, especially for portable and automotive applications where gravimetric and volumetric efficiencies are of utmost importance. Figure 14  Challenges for hydrogen energy components. Reproduced from [ 6 ] under CC BY license.

From the economic and durability aspects, things like expensive production, complicated synthesis methods, and the use of rare or expensive alloying elements are among the main obstacles that prevent the commercialization of the products. It is, therefore, very important that the manufacture should be carried out in a simplified and scalable manner using low-cost and readily available materials. Besides, hydride systems should be able to withstand changes in temperature, high pressure, and exposure to the environment, such as oxidation or corrosion. The key issue that still exists is the trade-off between cost, efficiency, and resistance properties, thus highlighting the need for combining material and system-level solutions to make metal hydride-based hydrogen storage technologies practical.

sections.heading: Material-related issues
paragraphs: Limited Storage Capacity  While complex hydrides offer high gravimetric capacities (4–20 wt%. Intermetallic hydrides typically have lower usable hydrogen capacities (less than 2 wt%). Achieving the U.S. DOE technical system target for onboard hydrogen storage for light-duty fuel cell vehicles, which is 6.5 wt% (equating to 7.02 kg of hydrogen in a 108 kg system), remains a significant challenge for many metal hydride materials [ 93 ].

High Absorption/Desorption Temperatures and Slow Kinetics  Many metal hydrides, especially complex hydrides, require high temperatures (often above 200 °C, or even 300 °C for borohydrides) for hydrogen discharge and high pressures (above 50 bar) for absorption. These physical and chemical properties of the metal hydrides, along with their generally slow kinetics, make them less desirable in terms of their use for applications that require fast charge and discharge [ 74 ]. For example, Mg2Ni has very slow hydrogen kinetics, and high operating conditions are required in order for it to operate [ 88 ].

Low Thermal Conductivity  Metal hydride materials exhibit a low thermal conductivity [ 88 ]. which significantly affects the transfer of heat within the storage system needed for the exothermic absorption and endothermic desorption processes [ 89 ,  93 ]. Poor heat transfer cause’s slow reaction rates and reduced overall performance of the system.

Material Degradation and Cyclic Stability  As metal hydrides go through multiple absorption and desorption cycles, they physically and chemically degrade, causing a reduction of the amount of storage capacity over time [ 88 ,  129 ]. The difference in specific volume between metal and hydride phases contributes to the degradation of the metal hydride powder through expansion/contraction, along with subsequent swelling, loss of compaction and fracture of the crystals, which will eventually affect the long-term stability of the material [ 88 ]. Surface contamination may cause damage (loss of capacity) and retardation (loss of kinetics) as well as corrosion, greatly reducing overall performance [ 129 ].

Cost of Raw Materials  Highly efficient high-performance metal hydrides, such as rare-earth metal hydrides (LaNi5), can be rather costly and may be scarce [ 88 ]. Similarly, the costs associated with the manufacture of metal hydrides with the AB2 composition are also considered high, owing to the expensive components used [ 27 ].

Safety Concerns  Although the potential of explosions is considerably lower for metal hydrides than for high-pressure hydrogen storage, certain metal hydrides will ignite upon exposure to air when there is a leak. Toxicity and inhalation of dust particles in powder form are also potential health hazards. Generating explosive gases such as boron hydrides in borohydride decomposition, is one more safety issue that should be addressed [ 129 ].

sections.heading: System-level issues
paragraphs: Thermal Management  Proper thermal management of metal hydride hydrogen storage systems is essential for the optimal performance of hydrogen absorption and desorption due to their highly temperature-dependent reactions. If heat is not properly managed, there will be hot or cold areas within the reactor that will reduce the overall absorption rate of hydrogen and may even lead to damaging high temperature levels. In most reactor designs, there are heat exchangers that help to maintain a more uniform reactor temperature distribution and facilitate the function of the hydrogen storage system.
Refueling Time  Because fast refueling times are a concern in mobile applications, new designs will be needed for thermal management systems or multiple tanks must be exchanged to resolve this issue.

Volume and Mass  Metal hydride volumetric density creates a size-to-weight problem with regard to the weight of storage, but may not create a problem with regard to height or length. If the tank is being designed and built for a mobile application where weight is critical, then the design of the tank must be optimized so that the maximum possible amount of storage space is available while also adhering to height/length vs. weight.

Tank Design and Material Compatibility  The container geometry/size/shape/material affect the pressure and temperature control of metal hydride materials. Containers must be made from materials that are compatible with the specific hydride being used in order to prevent chemical degradation/corrosion/chemical reactions. Stainless steel is one of the most common materials due to its high mechanical strength and corrosion-resistant properties. In addition, tanks submerged in the water will also need to support the external forces acting on them.

sections.heading: Advanced hydride reactor design and thermal management strategies
paragraphs: The design of the metal hydride reactor is important for proper thermal control of the system. Absorption of hydrogen as a gas and desorption of hydrogen as a gas are both highly exothermic and endothermic reactions, respectively. Reactor design therefore, plays a critical role in regulating temperature distribution, reaction kinetics, and ultimately efficiency [ 236 ,  237 ].

Heat Exchanger Design in Hydride Reactors  Typically, hydride reactors are constructed with embedded heat exchangers to control temperatures during hydrogen cycling. Common reactor design configurations for the heat exchangers include embedded tubular exchangers, shell and tube exchangers, and microchannel heat exchangers. Embedded cooling/heating tubes in the hydride bed provide direct access to heat generated or consumed during the reaction, creating very small thermal gradients and improving uniformity of reaction products. Advanced heat exchanger designs utilizing microchannel technology provide a very high surface area to volume ratio, allowing for rapid removal of heat from the hydride bed and superior thermal response. These reactor configurations have a distinct advantage when processing high-capacity hydrides like Magnesium Hydride, as they help overcome heat transfer limitations that severely restrict performance [ 238 ,  239 ].

Hydride Bed Architectures  The internal structure of the hydride bed has a large impact on both heat transfer and mass transfer processes. Conventional packed powder beds typically have limited thermal conductivity and have poor heat dissipation capabilities. To mitigate this issue, several engineered internal architectures have been proposed including finned structures (metallic fins embedded within the hydride bed) to improve radial heat transfer and minimize temperature gradients during operation. ii) Metal Foams: The use of open-cell metal foams, for example, aluminum and copper foams, results in a very conductive porous medium that is conducive to both heat and hydrogen transfer. iii) Porous Media and Structured Beds: Lattice structures formed through additive manufacturing technologies can control flow paths and facilitate efficient transport processes.
Such structures improve reactor performance through reduction of localized hot spots and enhancement of hydrogen uptake/release kinetics [ 240 ,  241 ].

Thermally Enhanced Composite Materials  Composite Hydride Materials with Improved Thermal Conductivity: One method to increase the effective thermal conductivity of hydride materials is to develop composite materials that possess both a hydride matrix and an effective means of interconnecting the particles of the matrix. To do this, we typically use various materials such as expanded graphite, graphene, carbon nanotubes, and metal powders (such as Al and Cu) to create conductivity networks in the hydride matrix. Not only do these materials improve heat transfer, but they also improve the dispersion of particles and the structural integrity of the composite during repeated cycles of heating and cooling. Graphene-based composites have shown significant increases in thermal conductivity and hydrogen sorption kinetics compared to their respective parent materials, making them very promising candidates for use in commercial hydride-reactor systems [ 241 ,  242 – 243 ].

Reactor Modeling and Simulation Approaches  Reactor Modeling and Simulation Techniques: In order to maximize the performance of hydride reactors, there are an increasing number of advanced techniques being developed for modeling and simulating the performance of the reactors. These techniques include: i) Computational fluid dynamics (CFD): CFD is typically used to model the heat and mass transfer in hydride materials and to predict the temperature distribution and flow patterns within the hydride bed; ii) MP Models: Multi-physics (MP) models couple the thermodynamics, kinetics, and heat transfer in the reactor to predict the actual performance of the reactor in real-time; iii) Kinetic Thermal Coupled Models: Kinetic thermal coupled models developed allow for the prediction of the absorption/desorption kinetics of hydrogen gas under varying operating conditions. These modeling techniques provide important information to aid in the optimization of the reactors by providing designers with a means to evaluate various geometries, materials, and operating conditions without requiring numerous costly and time-consuming experimental trials [ 244 ,  245 ].

sections.heading: Environmental sustainability and life cycle considerations of metal hydrides
Life cycle emissions of metal hydride systems
paragraphs: To evaluate the environmental impact of hydrogen storage methods, you cannot look only at the emissions produced during the operation of those methods. An LCA is needed for the entire life cycle of the technology to properly assess its impacts. These emissions differ depending on the technology used, and different technologies have different effects on the environment. For example, metal hydride hydrogen storage systems have close to zero emissions during the storage and release of hydrogen. However, because of the upstream processes (e.g., raw material extraction, alloy manufacturing and processing), these metal hydride systems have a significant carbon footprint [ 246 ].

For example, magnesium hydrides use less embodied energy per mass than rare-earth intermetallic hydrides because magnesium is abundant whereas mining and refining rare-earth elements is energy-intensive. Furthermore, the high-temperature synthesis methods used for these systems (i.e., melt spinning and mechanical alloying) require energy-consuming processes that produce indirect emissions. Therefore, although using metal hydrides will result in cleaner hydrogen, the overall emissions associated with using metal hydrides will vary considerably depending on the materials selected and the paths taken to process those materials for use in hydrogen storage. In order to reduce the overall environmental burden of hydrides, the entrances to these technologies should be entered with low-energy renewable-powered techniques or routes [ 247 ,  248 – 249 ].

sections.heading: Recycling and regeneration of hydride materials
paragraphs: Another important consideration for the long-term sustainability of hydrogen storage materials is their recyclability. Reversible metal hydride hydrogen storage systems demonstrate a relatively high ability to meet their performance characteristics through multiple cycles of hydrogen absorption and desorption, as evidenced by the intermetallic and magnesium-based systems, and they will not lose a significant amount of the material through those cycles. However, degradation mechanisms such as oxidation, phase segregation, and pulverization can reduce recyclability over extended cycles [ 8 ,  250 ].

The use of chemical hydrides presents a higher level of difficulty since they involve an irreversible path of reactions, hence necessitating regeneration that is carried out off-board in many cases and involves considerable energy expenditure and cost. For instance, used borohydrides and ammonia borane hydrides must be chemically recycled, which may negate any positive environmental impact they bring about. However, emerging technologies like closed-loop systems, catalytic regeneration, and nanoscale hydride storage could make a difference here [ 251 ,  252 ].

sections.heading: Critical raw material dependency
paragraphs: Metal Hydrides and Sustainability Issues: Raw Material Availability.

In addition to technological constraints, metal hydride sustainability issues are affected by the availability of key raw materials and their geopolitical distribution. High-performance metal hydrides contain such raw materials as rare-earth metals (lanthanum, cerium), transition metals (nickel, cobalt), and strategic alloying metals (zirconium, niobium). For instance, AB5-type hydrides require large amounts of rare-earth metals, while new catalysts may contain cobalt or nickel. These two types of raw materials are considered critical [ 253 ].

To address this issue, current research is focusing on: Developing low cost and earth-abundant alternatives (e.g., Mg-based systems) Reducing reliance on critical elements through compositional optimization Exploring high-entropy alloys with flexible elemental substitution
Such strategies are essential for ensuring sustainable deployment at an industrial scale.

sections.heading: Environmental impact of synthesis processes
paragraphs: The synthesis and treatment of metal hydrides are crucial aspects that determine the environmental impact. The traditional methods used in manufacturing metal hydrides include ball milling, arc melting, and chemical synthesis methods, which consume large amounts of energy and can use harmful chemicals or inert environments. For example, ball milling is an energy-consuming process that takes a lot of time, and the production of chemical hydrides may produce some toxic intermediates or waste products. Furthermore, nanostructuring methods, although useful in enhancing kinetic performance, could also raise environmental issues [ 254 ,  255 ].

To mitigate these impacts, sustainable synthesis strategies are being explored, including: Green chemistry approaches for hydride preparation Low-temperature and solvent-free synthesis techniques Utilization of renewable energy sources during processing Development of scalable and environmentally benign manufacturing routes
These advancements are crucial for aligning hydrogen storage technologies with global sustainability targets.

sections.heading: Overall sustainability outlook
paragraphs: Although metal hydrides present a safe and efficient means of storing hydrogen, sustainability in relation to this technology requires a harmonious combination of performance, abundance, recyclability, and ecological compatibility. Future research should be based on an integrated strategy that focuses both on material development and life cycle management [ 8 ,  256 ].

sections.heading: Applications of metal hydrides for hydrogen storage
paragraphs: Hydrides of metals play an important role in the development of hydrogen energy technology, where hydrogen is safely stored in a solid and reversible manner, as shown in Fig.  15 . In the case of energy systems based on renewable energy sources, hydrogen generated via electrolysis of water under solar or wind energy can be stored in hydrides. Hydrogen stored using metal hydride technology can be constructed at room temperature with moderate pressure, therefore providing a higher volumetric density and a safer gas than when using compressed or liquefied hydrogen. Due to their high volumetric density, they also lend themselves to being used for stationary energy storage systems for buffering energy requirements and stabilizing the electrical grid during energy supply fluctuations from renewable sources. Another benefit of metal hydrides is their ability to provide seasonally long-term storage capabilities for hydrogen, which when combined with underground hydrogen storage, can be used to deliver a reliable source of energy to support industrial, residential, and utility applications. Figure 15 Schematic representation of the hydrogen ecosystem from production to storage modalities, and end-use applications. Reproduced from [ 257 ] under CC BY license.

In addition to stationary applications, metal hydrides are being considered for on-demand hydrogen delivery for fuel cells and hydrogen-powered vehicles due to their ability to release hydrogen when desired under specific temperature-controlled conditions. Due to their versatility, they can also be used as supplemental onboard hydrogen storage tanks for buses, automobiles, and portable power systems, thereby connecting the hydrogen production and the use of hydrogen as an energy carrier. In addition to transportation uses, metal hydrides can also be used for backup power systems, in the aerospace industry, and for hydrogen refueling infrastructure where high reliability and safety are critical. Overall, as demonstrated in Fig.  14 , metal hydrides can play an important role in supporting a transition to a sustainable energy future by linking the production of renewable hydrogen, its efficient storage, and its diverse end-uses across the residential, transportation and industrial sectors.

sections.heading: Stationary applications
paragraphs: In stationary hydrogen storage, metal hydrides have unique advantages in terms of energy density per volume, safety, and low-pressure operation. These materials can readily absorb and release hydrogen at moderate temperatures and pressures, making them suitable for stationary hydrogen energy management and storage applications. Consequently, they are applicable in renewable energy storage applications and backup power generation [ 129 ].

Home Storage Systems  Residential Hydrogen Storage Systems: Metal Hydrides such as Titanium-iron (TiFe) and Lanthanum-nickel (LaNi₅)-based alloys are ideal for use as a home-based Hydrogen Storage Solution when combined with photovoltaic solar systems or small-scale wind turbines, because they operate at temperatures below 100 °C [ 258 ]. Because they can be used for the on-site storage of hydrogen to be utilized later via fuel cells or home heating systems, this product allows for a maintenance-free and compact source of hydrogen that produces no noise during operation and has relatively low safety risks [ 140 ].

Power-to-Power (P2P) Systems  The use of metal hydride storage tanks between electrolyzers and fuel cells in a Power-to-Power (P2P) system creates a complete closed-loop energy conversion system. Hydrogen produced from renewable energy sources is stored as a metal hydride and subsequently released from the storage tank to generate electricity as needed. The maximum operating (outlet) pressure of PEM electrolyzers (approximately 30 bar) is compatible with the absorption characteristics exhibited by many metal hydrides, allowing for the elimination of energy-intensive compressor technologies [ 129 ]. PEM fuel cells require a desorption pressure range of 3–5 bars which is consistent with the desorption pressure of many metal hydride storage systems, thereby facilitating an efficient integration of the two systems, as well as ultimately decreasing the overall cost of the system by simplifying many of the balance-of-plant components associated with the two systems [ 129 ].

Medium-Scale Energy Storage  For moderate scale operations between 100 kWh and 100 MWh, there is also the potential use of metal hydrides like sodium aluminum hydride (NaAlH 4 ) or magnesium hydrides, which have higher capacities and better thermodynamics. This technology can be applied in renewable power grid stabilization, microgrids, or community energy storage where thermal management and constant delivery of hydrogen are needed [ 84 ,  258 ].

Bulk Hydrogen Storage  Metal hydrides present a viable option compared to the cryogenic and compressed alternatives for bulk energy storage, as they minimize losses due to evaporation and do not require bulky tanks for containment [ 84 ]. With this technology, seasonal or utility-level energy management is possible since hydrogen gas can be stored for extended periods with no appreciable loss. Despite this, large capacities involving hundreds of MWh pose problems of weight, raw materials costs, and heat issues [ 215 ]. Despite this disadvantage, the high volumetric energy density and modularity of metal hydrides make them a suitable choice for stationary energy storage applications at different scales [ 125 ].

sections.heading: Transportation applications
paragraphs: Research into the use of metal hydride materials for use in transportation has been ongoing since the late 1960s, with the desire to find a viable alternative to the currently impractical compressed or liquefied hydrogen options available today for the delivery of hydrogen fuel for use in the transportation industry [ 27 ].

Rail and Marine Transportation  Rail and marine transportation have both certain characteristics that would provide an excellent storage medium for the hydrogen fuel needed for these applications. Certain metal hydride alloys, such as TiFe-type alloys and LaNi-5-type alloys, have operational temperature ranges of below 100 °C and therefore are both safe to use and offer a high degree of compactness when used for hydrogen storage in either application. In the case of rail transportation, metal hydride storage modules can easily be integrated into rail propulsion systems with fuel cell stacks, providing continuous power generation with minimal vibration or noise. Therefore, providing a highly efficient, low-emission alternative to current diesel-electric locomotives. For marine applications, it is physically possible to store hydrogen in hydride tanks at pressures less than 30 bar, significantly reducing the potential for explosion hazard, and thus simplifying the refueling processes at the docks for refueling ships. With regards to long voyage sea-going vessels, the onboard thermal management systems can utilize the energy created from combustion processes, used onboard the ship, as well as thermal energy from onboard thermal systems, to actively manage the release or absorption of hydrogen from the hydride tanks, thus improving the overall energy efficiency of the ship [ 258 ].

Maritime Sector  This is generally regarded as one of the most promising avenues for the development of metal hydrides. Refueling infrastructure at ports would be less expensive than conventional gas or liquid forms of Hydrogen because it would allow for much lower pressure to be maintained during operation, leading to greater efficiencies with respect to hydrogen fuel cell vessels. For example, Germany’s submarine (Type 212) and derivatives are examples of early adopters of using metal hydride systems in the maritime industry, as can be the disadvantages of batteries from their size and weight. There are several examples of vessels using metal hydride systems to power them, including the Ross Barlow (4 kg H 2  stored in AB 2  alloys shipped in 2007); the Zero Emission Ultimate Ship (ZEUS), also by Fincanitare; and the Bi- Innovative & Modular Hybrid Boat (BIIM) from AB 5  modules with 6 KG H 2  in ship modules (52 KG shipped in 2023) [ 27 ].

Non-Road Vehicles  There is a growing demand for the application of metal hydrides in non-road transportation, particularly in forklifts, airport ground-support vehicles, mining machinery and agricultural equipment. These types of vehicles are generally used in areas where low-level emissions or noise are required, as well as safety; therefore, hydride-based hydrogen storage systems have advantages over both compressed and liquid hydrogen systems. The operating pressures (typically 5–20 bar) provide an additional level of safety, while the ability to replace modular tanks allows for uninterrupted operation without extended refueling times. In addition, hydride materials are thermally stable and reversible, which will allow for rapid cycling of hydrogen; therefore, metal hydrides are a viable alternative for industrial mobility systems where there is a need for reliable and long-lasting performance [ 258 ].

Road Applications  The application of metal hydride systems to road transportation is very widespread, with several different types of prototypes being developed for 2-, 3-, and 4-wheel mobility. While the traditional drawback of weight is an issue, in the case of lightweight (for example, two-wheel) vehicles, metal hydride systems can be advantageous because they typically can store significant amounts of hydrogen onboard if compressed gas tanks may not prove practical. A number of different examples exist, including hydrogen-powered fuel cell electric bicycles which contain approximately 7 g of hydrogen storage. In general, metal hydrides are superior to other similar battery-powered electric vehicle technologies when comparing medium to heavy-duty vehicles, such as those used in utility-type applications. At this point, though, low refueling times continue to present a major disadvantage and require effective thermal management systems as well as tank swap-out alternatives [ 27 ].

sections.heading: Other applications
paragraphs: Metal hydrides, apart from being the principal hydrogen storage media, are increasingly being used for a number of thermodynamic and other application purposes due to their unique, reversible hydrogen absorption and desorption processes as well as their favorable thermal characteristics.

Metal Hydride Compressors  Metal hydride compressors take advantage of the absorption and desorption processes to create pressure differencing in order to effectively and mechanically compress hydrogen gas to several tens of MPa. These systems are especially promising for stationary and distributed hydrogen infrastructure since they are quiet, require little maintenance, and can operate using waste heat or low-level thermal sources, such as solar collector systems, for their thermal energy. The absence of wear components allows for a longer service life from a reliability perspective, particularly when compared to metal mechanical compressors.

Metal Hydride Heat Pumps  Metal hydride heat pumps operate through thermochemical processes, which involve two hydride beds that are at different temperature and pressure ranges. Both the exothermic absorption and endothermic desorption processes are utilized to transfer heat from one end to another, which provide heating or cooling processes to the system without the use of refrigerants. They are extremely energy efficient and environmentally friendly. They can also be powered through waste heat from industrial processes or through solar processes. The solid-state construction of these systems means that they can be devoid of mechanical components, which makes them ideal for applications such as waste heat recovery as well as air conditioning and temperature management of renewable energy systems.

Purification and Separation  Due to their unique absorption characteristics, metal hydrides can be employed for the purification of hydrogen, as well as for the separation of hydrogen isotopes (protium, deuterium, and tritium) through selective absorption. During the desorption and absorption of the hydride, hydrogen can be purified to very high levels without needing to resort to cryogenic or membrane-based separation systems. This is advantageous in the purification of hydrogen in industrial hydrogen recycle systems as well as in nuclear and fusion research facilities.

Thermal Storage  Metal hydrides can store and put forth thermal energy due to the high enthalpy of their hydride formation. As they function similarly to phase change materials, they can be used for thermal regulation purposes. The heating effect that results from the adsorption process can be harvested for other uses. On the other hand, the heat that is produced during the desorption process may facilitate thermal regulation and stabilization. With these features in mind, metal hydrides can be used for thermal management of energy hybrid systems and concentrated solar power plants.

sections.heading: Integration challenges and innovation
paragraphs: While hydrides provide excellent volumetric units of hydrogen and are also reversible, several interdependent technical barriers have limited their real-world applications. These barriers include poor thermal management, which is really the major bottleneck in hydrogen storage. The heat produced by the hydrogen being adsorbed (as a result of an exothermic reaction) reduces the speed at which hydrogen can be adsorbed and can also cause instability if this heat is not allowed to disperse quickly enough. On the other hand, the hydrogen being released from those same hydrides is an endothermic process, requiring heat to be provided from an external source before hydrogen is released [ 259 ,  260 ]. For example, when examining magnesium hydride (MgH 2 ), the temperature required for desorption is 250–300 °C by virtue of Industrial Standards, which is too high for most mobile or distributed energy applications. This adds to the complexity of those systems and piles additional energy costs onto the wireline compared to compressed gas/cylinder formats. Other barriers are kinetic and reversible; for example, many complex hydrides theoretically can contain very high amounts of hydrogen. However, the diffusion is slow and multiple steps would also result in slow and inefficient hydrogen release rates, making these systems not applicable for large-scale commercial applications. Ways that can be utilized for enhancing the reaction pathways to allow better performance include: prudent alloying, catalysis, and microstructure engineering [ 250 ].

From a molecular standpoint, some of the primary issues relate to both material and cyclic stability. In terms of metal hydrides, it would be an ideal characteristic for them to undergo several rounds of hydriding and dehydriding without any notable decline in performance capacity [ 250 ]. Some of the common difficulties encountered include structural modifications, phase transitions, and particle agglomeration. Nano-structuring strategies, such as embedding hydrides in porous scaffolds or mixing them with high thermal-conductivity additives (e.g., graphite), are being explored worldwide to overcome these limitations and increase industrial scalability [ 24 ,  261 ]. sections.heading: Safety, durability, and system economics
paragraphs: One of the significant safety benefits of metal hydrides is that much of the hydrogen will be stored in a chemically bound state and hence at much lower pressures than in gaseous hydrogen tanks. This significantly lowers the stored energy and eliminates the potential for rapid depressurization incidents. However, metal hydrides are not completely hazard free since there is a transfer of risks from mostly pressure-based hazards to thermochemical and other hazards [ 125 ,  220 ,  221 ,  222 – 223 ].

While MH beds do not experience thermal runaway similar to batteries, fast hydrogen loading may lead to self-heating due to hydriding. Heat dissipation is important to avoid hot spots, where temperature and pressure in the bed increase, inhibiting further loading of hydrogen, destabilizing neighboring areas, and leading to overpressure in extreme scenarios. In particular, the poor thermal conductivity of most hydride beds (~ 0.1–0.3 W/m K) exacerbates the problem. Proper cooling, addition of heat-conductive material, moderate loading rate, and appropriate pressure relief measures are necessary [ 220 ,  221 ,  224 ].

However, hydrogen leaks must be accounted for even in MH systems, which have a smaller amount of freely compressed hydrogen as compared to CGH 2  containers, making the immediate impact of such leaks somewhat less. The reasons for hydrogen leaks may be valves, seals, manifolds, welding seams, and venting, particularly due to repeated thermal cycling. However, MH systems will also require hydrogen sensors, venting, leak-tight joints, leak tests upon commissioning, and segregation from igniting sources. Designing the vessel will have to account for the maximum possible pressure when all the hydrogen is released from the material and also fires and overheating situations. Nevertheless, these criteria are relatively milder than those applied to CGH 2  vessels operating at 350–700 bar [ 220 ,  221 ,  222 – 223 ,  225 ].

Safety considerations become specific to the material in case of complex/chemical hydrides. Hydrides based on borohydride or alanate family and other high-capacity chemical compounds may generate toxic gases such as diborane, borazine, or ammonia upon dehydrogenation reactions, which may react with water or oxygen and cause further complications. Furthermore, even traces of these gases may damage the PEM fuel cell used in the process. For this reason, it is necessary to handle these materials in an inert atmosphere during synthesis, loading, maintenance, and disposal processes, as well as using downstream gas purification equipment in practical applications. On the other hand, intermetallic hydrides including LaNi 5 - and TiFe systems are generally safer for multiple cycles due to their mild operating conditions and non-decomposition process paths [ 125 ,  220 ,  226 ,  227 ].

Durability-wise, cycling between hydriding and dehydriding could lead to pulverization, sintering, phase separation, contamination, and loss of thermal contact with the heat transfer medium. These factors will ultimately degrade system capacity, increase kinetic sluggishness, and potentially affect the relationship between reactor pressure and temperature. Cost-wise, besides the MH alloy itself, costs will include the heat exchanger, container, insulation, valves, sensors, instrumentation, and, if necessary, gas purifiers. This means that MH technology is particularly advantageous when space considerations and safety take precedence over gravimetric losses, such as stationary energy storage, emergency power sources, service fleet applications, and long-term hydrogen storage. Current technoeconomic assessments indicate that stationary MH systems can actually enjoy a land-use advantage over compressed hydrogen, despite being penalized by alloy costs and thermal management issues [ 84 ,  125 ,  224 ,  228 ].

sections.heading: Futuristic integration pathways
paragraphs: Despite challenges, several convergent innovations point toward realistic and commercially meaningful MH deployments when materials science, thermal engineering, and digital design are co-optimized [ 263 ]. Below are the principal pathways that can take MHs from laboratory curiosities to backbone elements of hydrogen infrastructures.

Materials engineering in the context of hydrogen storage aims at reducing reaction enthalpy and enhancing kinetics without compromising volumetric or gravimetric storage density. An example of this is magnesium hydride (MgH 2 ), which has a stoichiometric capacity of 7.6 wt.% H 2 , which has typically been desorbed at approximately 300 °C [ 264 ]. Due to the introduction of nanostructure engineering and catalytic doping by means of Nb 2 O 5  or Ti-based nanoparticle additives, the desorption temperatures of magnesium hydride have been reduced to well below 225 °C, resulting in the rates of hydrogen released being decreased from several hours to less than 15 min [ 265 ,  266 ]. Similarly, destabilized composite materials such as LiBH₄/MgH₂ have shown reductions in decompositional enthalpy of as much as 30–40 kJ/mol H 2 , thereby allowing the use of hydrogen from storage to be processed at the temperature limits of industrial waste heat. The numerical improvements achieved through this research are not simply incremental; they will change the boundary conditions that define the utility of hydrides for practical applications [ 267 ,  268 ].

Due to the evolution of digital technology, it has become possible for us to produce new forms of development through innovative ways (solutions and/or enhancements). As a result, there is sufficient evidence to show that new types or models based on the use of machine learning (ML) will be able to provide us with the tools needed for our experimental synthesis and/or experimentation identification/conceptualization processes to help develop predictive models (with accuracies of ± 0.1 log (P) for plateau pressures & ± 5 kJ·mol⁻ 1  H 2  for enthalpies—these accuracies are adequate for experimental synthesis guidance) [ 269 ]. Consequently, the reduction of time required for the experimental identification of new hydrides (previously 3–5 years for each candidate, now 2–3 months with some methods taking as little as 2–3 weeks from prediction to experimental verification) illustrates how successful we have become via learning new methods [ 270 ].

At the system level, integrating hydrides with thermal energy storage (TES) has proven to be a major avenue. In conventional hydride tanks, up to 30–40% of the reaction heat goes to waste into the environment [ 270 ]. MH–TES hybrid systems, however, recover this heat on absorption and recycle it for use during desorption, enhancing round-trip efficiency by 10–20 percentage points over individual MH beds [ 271 ]. For fixed installations, TES coupling has enabled demonstration modules with capacities ranging from 50 to 100 kg of H 2 , sufficient to power microgrids or industries for a few hours. Scaled future designs conceive multi-megawatt-hour seasonal storage facilities, where TES-augmented MH banks would level renewable intermittency over weeks, not hours [ 102 ,  272 ].

sections.heading: MH-thermal energy storage (TES) co-designed reactors: closed thermal loops
paragraphs: The clearest near route that is currently being developed is the tightly coupled MH-TES reactor: (Refer to Fig.  18  for the design of the reactor for advanced hydrogen storage). During hydrogen charging, the exothermic heat is stored in an adjacent sensible latent TES (e.g., high-temperature molten salt, phase-change ceramics, or thermochemical media); during the discharge cycle, that stored heat is returned to the hydride to drive desorption, reducing or eliminating external fuel inputs. When a TES is selected to match the hydride enthalpy and power demands, the reactor operates with a high degree of efficiency and autonomy which increases the trip efficiency, although engineering challenges remain, for instance minimizing TES mass for a given energy capacity, matching TES operating temperature to the hydride plateau and designing fast and reliable heat exchange, but recent experimental and modeling studies demonstrate compact modular units with promising energy as well as power densities that can be scaled from portable fuel packs to multi-MWh stationary banks. The existing literature shows prototype MH-TES systems that have achieved substantial reductions in external heating demands and improved cycle efficiency, which strongly suggests that this architecture is especially compelling for stationary seasonal storage and remote microgrids. Figure 18 Use of mechanical metamaterials reactor design for advanced hydrogen storage systems. Reprinted from [ 273 ], with permission from Elsevier.

sections.heading: Catalysis, destabilization and reactive composites for lower-temperature operation
paragraphs: Material strategies will continue to push desorption temperatures downward and reaction kinetics upward to make the process industrially benign [ 274 ]. Catalytic nanoparticles, through alloying, have already reduced practical desorption temperatures and improved reversible capacities in laboratories, but it is far from commercialization [ 275 ]. For instance, some catalysts lower the MgH 2  desorption onset by more than 100 °C and enable fast cycling at temperatures exceeding 200 °C in microstructurally engineered composites. Currently, these breakthroughs expand the usable suite of heat sources (e.g., low-grade waste heat, solar thermal collectors, etc.) and simplify their integration into vehicles and buildings. Current efforts continue to aim for high gravimetric density while avoiding irreversible side reactions and preserving cycle life [ 268 ,  275 ] (Fig.  19 ). Figure 19 Present and future use of catalysis in hydrogen storage. Reprinted from [ 276 ], with permission from Elsevier.

sections.heading: AI-driven inverse design and rapid PCT predictions
paragraphs: Data-driven methods accelerate the search for hydrides that simultaneously meet kinetic, enthalpy, and cost, as well as cyclability targets. Recently updated ML tools have the capacity to predict Pressure-Composition-Temperatures (PCT) isotherms, which clearly define the equilibrium conditions for hydrogen adsorption and release [ 277 ,  278 ]. ML algorithms trained on experimental datasets have achieved root mean square errors (RMSE) below 0.1 log (P), making them faster than DFT calculations. For example, the MH-PCT pro tool predicted the plateau pressures of AB 5 -type alloys, such as LaNi 5 H 6  and TiFeH 2 , with accuracies sufficient to guide synthesis, thereby reducing wet lab costs by more than an order of magnitude [ 217 ].

Beyond material thermodynamics and kinetics, ML has also been applied to supervise the design of destabilized hydride composites [ 279 ]. By analyzing and correlating large datasets of enthalpy changes and decomposition pathways, algorithms have proposed new combinations such as LiBH 4 –MgH 2  and NaAlH 4 –TiH 2 , where the new predicted destabilization principle reduces the desorption temperatures by 50–100 °C compared to the individual parent compounds. These predictions were, in fact, later validated experimentally, confirming that ML can successfully narrow down the vast array of plausible materials for viable destabilization partners [ 280 ].

Catalyst discovery is one of the many emerging frontiers. ML-guided methods have benefited the stationary hydrogen storage industry by highlighting previously unexplored transition metals such as Nb. Ti, V as particularly effective additives for improved MgH 2  desorption kinetics, with studies reporting a reduction in activation energy from > 160 kJ·mol⁻ 1  to < 100 kJ·mol⁻ 1  when there was deployment of carefully optimized nanoparticle dispersions [ 281 ,  282 ]. For instance, catalyzed MgH 2  samples have released more than 90% of their hydrogen within 10 min at 250 °C, compared to several hours for catalyzed materials. This shows quantitative improvements that translate directly into shorter desorption times [ 283 ,  284 ].

The culmination of active learning loops—where ML models are continuously refined by continuous feedback from new experimental or computational results—has further accelerated the laboratory progress [ 285 ,  286 ]. In some recent works, there has been a suggestion of alloys by ML that could be synthesized and tested within 2–3 weeks, compared to the rigorous traditional cycle of hypothesis modeling, synthesis, and validation. High-throughput ML models have already identified families in Ti-Cr-Mn alloys and mixed alanates that exhibit promising thermodynamic profiles for onboard vehicle storage [ 105 ].

sections.heading: Modular hybrid networks: MHs as buffers
paragraphs: Instead of replacing all hydrogen modes, MHs will likely occupy complementary roles within hybrid networks. In mobility, fast kinetic intermetallics with integrated TES could serve as compact onboard buffers that smooth fuel cell transients and enable a rapid, near-liquid fueling profile.

sections.heading: Renewable heat integration and distributed production
paragraphs: An appealing futuristic scientific vision pairs localized renewable hydrogen production (electrolysis) with co-located MH TES storage: surplus midday solar powers electrolysis; just like a symbiotic relationship in exchange, the hydride charges while its absorption heat is stored in TES; overnight, the TE-assisted hydride supplies hydrogen to fuel cells with little additional input. In another variant, concentrated solar thermal collectors provide the desorption heat directly to specially engineered hydrides with plateau temperatures tailored to the solar flux. Recent demonstrators show solar-driven desorption of catalyzed MgH 2  at practical rates, opening pathways for distributed, fuel-free hydrogen dispatch [ 127 ,  287 ].

sections.heading: Design targets, policy, and manufacturing pathways
paragraphs: Being a fairly new framework, the long-term success of metal hydride-TES systems will depend on setting realistic yet ambitious design and development targets. On the material side, hydrides must present the correct enthalpy and plateau pressure values and pressures to match available heat sources, enabling the charging and discharging processes to be driven by low-grade waste heat or any renewable thermal energy source [ 85 ,  288 ,  289 ].

Catalysts should be optimized to increase the rates while remaining stable through thousands of adsorption and desorption cycles to keep the fuel cell efficacy for years [ 15 ,  290 ,  291 ]. Bed architectures should also be optimized to increase the thermal conductivity through foams, fins, or composite structures to reach the required power densities without facing an excessive mass or volume penalty [ 292 ]. Manufacturing approaches for hydride powders, composite beds, and system-integrated reactor modules should be developed to be scalable and cost-effective.

In terms of government policies, the procurement framework, which will ultimately decide when hydrogen and fuel cells are a reality, should be more flexible to enable alterations in policy regarding factors such as inherent safety and compact land use, rather than simply the price per kilogram saved. Furthermore, looking ahead to future policies, planning for the recycling of waste from the hydrogen fuel cells based on the metal hydride as part of the future infrastructure should also be a priority.
