sections.heading: Future outlook and recommendations
paragraphs: The future for advanced metal hydrides in green hydrogen storage has much potential, but also many hurdles to overcome. Metal hydrides remain a top contender as the best light-duty hydrogen storage medium due to their high volumetric and gravimetric energy density, volumetric safety, and the ease with which they could be integrated into renewable energy processes. This is assuming we can develop hydrides with better gravimetric and volumetric capacity, improve their kinetics and thermodynamics, reduce their dependence on critical minerals, and develop manufacturing technology away from the lab to the real world. The most recent breakthroughs include using artificial intelligence and machine learning to discover and optimize materials far faster, developing new hybrid systems that combine both physical and chemical storage, and conducting life cycle studies to ensure sustainability.

With regard to the discovery and optimization of metal hydrides, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and MXene integrated hydrides provide customizable characteristics and enhanced hydrogen uptake and release kinetics. AI-driven advanced screening enables swift identification of promising candidates through the identification of essential performance-influencing features and customization of material compositions for particular applications, thus substantially reducing the need for expensive and time-intensive experimental trials. For example, ML frameworks have been employed for predicting hydrogen storage findings for LaNi-type reactors, selecting optimum alloy compositions for fuel cells, and guiding the synthesis of high-entropy alloy (HEA) hydrides with desired thermodynamic properties, as found experimentally to verify prediction accuracy. Varying types of ML models, such as decision trees, random forests, neural networks, and ensemble methods, have been effectively employed to predict hydrogen storage capacities and optimum operating parameters for a series of hydride materials that include intermetallics, high-entropy alloys, as well as complex hydrides. Meanwhile, first-principle calculations and molecular dynamics simulations provide insights into thermodynamics and kinetics. Apart from the discovery of new materials, AI and ML are also being integrated into designing and optimizing metal hydride storage systems. Machine learning models presently can forecast how reactor shape, the ways heat is dealt with, and how a facility runs affect how well hydrogen is kept in storage; this lets researchers create really good, cheap ways to store hydrogen. The use of mixed modeling—using what is found in tests, computer modeling, and machine learning methods—has made it more precise to understand what a system does and to get the best settings for a variety of uses. Improved systems, however, continue to have difficulties; for example, quality issues, comprehension of model output, and issues associated with integrating machine learning techniques with experimental methodologies remain. The advancement of AI-driven hydrogen storage will require standardization of data acquisition processes and development of large, publicly accessible databases. Collaboration among scientists from diverse disciplines will facilitate the construction of AI-driven hydrogen storage more readily and enhance the development of environmentally friendly hydrogen storage solutions.

Systems that put together metal hydrides and either compressed or liquefied hydrogen storage are now more and more seen to have a better energy density and be more flexible. These kinds of systems use both the great storage density of hydrides and the quick charging and discharging of physical storage. To get these systems to work on a bigger scale and to make them work more efficiently, it is vital to combine them with thermal energy storage (TES) and good heat management. Projects to show how they work, and commercial uses—for example, hydrogen-electric energy storage systems and uses in the sea—are becoming more common. The use of metal hydride storage in local power production, fixed power stations and transport systems is hopeful, especially for making the grid stable and for providing power if the mains fail. If you look at what they are for, systems that put metal hydrides with materials that change phase, or compressed gas, are being looked at for big, and offshore applications. Using heat which would otherwise be wasted, from fuel cells and renewable sources, could also help system efficiency and cut running costs.

Assessments of a product’s entire life, life cycle assessments, or sustainability studies, serve to judge the environmental effects, ability to be recycled, and financial viability of metal hydride storage systems. Key considerations are the origin of raw materials, the amount of energy used, how long the system lasts, and what happens to it when it is no longer useful. Hydrides founded on magnesium, and complex hydrides, are recognized for being plentiful and having little poisonous effect, although the continuing difficulty is getting the number of times they can be used, and their price, to be better. Studies combining technical and economic factors indicate that metal hydride systems can be as cheap as storing gas at high pressure; this is especially true if they are made to suit a particular purpose and are produced in large volumes. Nevertheless, the effect on the environment of gases which contribute to the greenhouse effect given off while the materials are made and the systems are running, has to be lessened by using production methods that do not damage the environment, and by recycling. To increase research and development, build the necessary infrastructure, and introduce the newest hydride storage technologies, we need government rules, encouragement for the market, and regulatory help. Japan and the European Union have made determined plans for hydrogen, backing trials and efforts to make products available to buy. There is a need for additional research on materials science, engineering, and data science in order to develop new hydrides and system designs. More information is still required to determine how long these substances remain stable, how they react after multiple uses, and how safe they are when used under real-world conditions.

sections.heading: Hydrogen-based cars worldwide: current status, comparative analysis, and research insights
paragraphs: The current status of hydrogen vehicles is that fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEV) are of great relevance to achieving “zero emission” mobility. They are advantageous for applications/functions/uses that are not suitable for B.E.V.s. An example of an application where F.C.E.V.s have advantages over B.E.V.s is long driving distances/long battery discharge cycles, cold weather performance, and/or rapid refueling needs [ 295 ,  296 ]. Unlike B.E.V.s, which rely on large lithium-ion battery packs for storing energy, F.C.E.V.s generate their own power using a PEM fuel cell by combusting (with oxygen from the air) the hydrogen that is stored in their tanks, thus producing only water vapor as an exhaust emission (Fig.  22 ) [ 297 ,  298 ]. Commercial sales of this technology began in the mid-2010s, but relative to B.E.V.s, F.C.E.V. sales to date have been modest; however, F.C.E.V. sales are continuing to increase in targeted markets, including California, Japan, South Korea and Europe [ 299 ,  300 ]. Figure 22 Fuel cell vehicle with onboard storage. Reprinted from [ 297 ], with permission from elsevier.

In the years from 2025 to 2026, the total number of FCEVs will be less than 30,000, and they will still be restricted to those countries where there is a supply of hydrogen fuel. The most widespread FCEVs have been found in Japan, due to the early intervention of the government along with Toyota’s innovations, then South Korea (Hyundai), and the USA (California). Europe has made rapid progress with its Hydrogen Strategy by the EU, while China prefers heavy-duty vehicles. The recurring themes in all research papers point out the benefits of FCEVs due to high energy density and quick refueling times (3–5 min versus 20–60 min for BEVs). However, the disadvantages are associated with high hydrogen production costs and limited infrastructure [ 301 ,  302 ] (Fig.  23 ). Figure 23 Fuel cell vehicle (FCV) sales volume. Reprinted from [ 303 ], with permission from elsevier.

The two major production FCEVs that are used for passenger cars include the Toyota Mirai (Generation II, released in 2020/2021) and the Hyundai Nexo (released in 2018, with updates until 2025). The BMW iX5 Hydrogen is still in limited pilot fleet operations (approximately 100 units worldwide by 2025), while the Honda CR-V e: FCEV (plug-in hybrid FCEV) was limitedly manufactured in 2025. All these vehicles use PEMFC stacks that operate at low temperatures (60–80 °C) and a hydrogen storage pressure of 700 bar using carbon-fiber composite tanks [ 304 ].

With more than 20,000 Mirai FCEVs sold worldwide, the Toyota Mirai is considered to be the most developed FCEV currently available. The second-generation Mirai’s fuel cell system is made up of a 128 kW PEMFC stack combined with a 182 hp electric motor. The tri-tank system can hold roughly 5.6 kg of hydrogen (at 700 bar) and provides an EPA-estimated driving range of 402 to 650 miles (647 to 1,046 km), depending on trim level and operating environment conditions. The Mirai’s tested real-world efficiency (under mixed cycle conditions) was 100 to 120 km of travel for every kilogram of hydrogen consumed. Research performed on the Mirai demonstrates exceptional performance in cold climates and optimal power delivery, with only a small reduction in range at subzero temperatures, in comparison with BEVs [ 305 ,  306 ].

The Hyundai Nexo competes directly with the Mirai as a compact crossover SUV. The Nexo features a 95 kW PEMFC stack with three high-pressure tanks, capable of holding 6.33 to 6.69 kg of hydrogen, providing an EPA driving range of 380 to 414 miles (612 to 666 km) in new models from model years 2024 through 2026. The Nexo typically has an efficiency rating of 90 to 110 km of travel for each kg of H₂ consumed. Providing a crossover-style body configuration, the Nexo is considered to be more family-friendly than the Mirai. The Nexo has received upgrades that include increased power output and an increase in the hydrogen storage capacity of the fuel cell tanks. While comparison tests utilizing chassis dynamometers show the Nexo’s fuel cell system has a rapid response to changes in load, the Nexo’s urban efficiency is lower than the Mirai, due to the Nexo’s increased weight [ 307 ,  308 ].

The iX5 Hydrogen of BMW, which is based on the X5 platform, is an example of a premium car solution. The vehicle is fitted with a fuel cell stack supplied by Toyota, having a power capacity of 125 kW. The vehicle can travel from 313 to 400 miles (500 to 640 km) thanks to a 6 kg hydrogen tank. Testing in terms of reliability and endurance is performed on the Autobahn highway [ 309 ,  310 ].

The Honda CR-V e: FCEV (2025) is an innovative plug-in hybrid fuel cell vehicle, where the onboard PEMFC has a reduced capacity (about 100 kW), which is supported by the use of a battery for short journeys running fully electrically. While the hydrogen storage capacity has been reduced to about 4–5 kg, the overall distance covered is more than 270 miles (435 km) [ 311 ].

sections.heading: Comparative analysis across key metrics
paragraphs: When it comes to acceleration, all of the current hydrogen fuel cell electric vehicles provide between 8 and 10 s of 0–60 mph acceleration for everyday use (Mirai ~ 9.2 s, Nexo ~ 9.5 s and iX5 ~ 6–7 s in Sport mode). The major difference with how these vehicles fill up is that each of the models could fill its tanks in 3–5 min at 700 bar filling stations versus 20–40 min for 80% charge with the BEV fast chargers. For range in mixed use, the Mirai and Nexo (500—650 km on the highways), and cold weather performance tests (several LCAs and performance papers) have shown a 10–20% reduction in range with FCEVs and a 30–50% reduction with BEVs due to efficient use of waste heat [ 304 ,  308 ,  309 – 310 ].

The tank-to-wheel efficiency for present-day PEMFC systems yields 50–60% efficiency or translates into 90–120 km/kg hydrogen. The highway performance of the Mirai has the greatest efficiencies as a result of the streamlined design. Lifecycles (LCA) of FCEVs powered by green hydrogen are showing lower GHG emissions from well-to-wheel than BEVs that are dependent upon power from the grid. For example, when hydrogen is produced using renewable electrolysis, the average FCEV emits ~ 105 g CO2/km, whereas BEVs’ average emissions are between 141 and 185 g CO2/km [ 312 ].

The cost of FCEVs limits their distribution; they are comparatively priced with BEVs ($50,000–$70,000 for Mirai–$50,000, Nexo–$60,000) with hydrogen priced at $10–$15/kg currently. Putting these factors together yields a comparable operating cost with premium gasoline-powered vehicles but at a higher operating cost compared to BEVs. The key barrier for adoption is infrastructure: there are around 1,000 charging stations across the world, which are mostly found in California (over 300 stations), Japan (over 200 stations), and South Korea (over 150 stations).

Regional deployment highlights strategy disparities. The “Hydrogen Society” initiative of Japan has promoted Mirai with incentives and hydrogen stations. South Korea capitalizes on Hyundai’s vertical structure to develop Nexo fleets for public transportation. The Zero-Emission Vehicles mandate of California along with hydrogen hubs promotes both Mirai and Nexo models. Europe emphasizes heavy-duty fuel cell vehicles while also observing an increasing passenger demand through trials by BMW. India and Australia pilot small fleets for commercial purposes.

sections.heading: Advantages and limitations from a research perspective
paragraphs: Research indicates that fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs) have a competitive advantage in long-haul and cold-weather use due to their high tank-to-wheel efficiency and fast refueling capabilities, making them ideal for taxis, delivery vans, and intercity travel. However, research also notes several other disadvantages associated with FCEVs, including a high reliance on infrastructure, the high amount of platinum required to produce proton-exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs), and greenhouse gas emissions from the production of hydrogen (particularly if it is produced using gray or blue hydrogen). The scalability of FCEVs depends on reducing the cost of producing green hydrogen to less than $2/kg [ 310 ].

The focus on the future is on developing new-generation PEMFCs that have a much longer lifespan (greater than 8,000 h), use less platinum than in the current production of PEMFCs, and can be used with solid oxide fuel cells or alkaline fuel cells to create a synergetic benefit for stationary applications. The development of hybrid FCEV designs (e.g., Honda CR-V e: FCEV) will allow for bridging the gaps in infrastructure [ 307 ,  310 ].

sections.heading: Hydrogen-based fuel cells in nasa missions: focus on the artemis program – design, development, and future challenges
paragraphs: Hydrogen has been a cornerstone of NASA’s human spaceflight since the Apollo era. The Apollo command and service modules relied on alkaline fuel cells (AFCs) that combined liquid hydrogen (LH 2 ) and liquid oxygen (LO 2 ) to generate electricity, heat, and potable water for the crew. This legacy continued in the Space Shuttle program with improved AFCs. Today, hydrogen remains central to NASA’s Artemis program, which aims to return humans to the Moon sustainably and establish a long-term presence as a stepping stone to Mars. NASA Hydrogen History Informs World’s Hydrogen Future [ 313 ].

In Artemis missions, hydrogen serves two primary roles: (1) as a high-performance cryogenic propellant for the Space Launch System (SLS) rocket and (2) as a reactant in advanced fuel cells for power generation on crewed spacecraft and lunar landers. The SLS core stage is powered by four RS-25 engines that burn LH 2  and LO 2 , delivering the thrust needed to escape Earth’s gravity. The world’s largest liquid hydrogen storage sphere at Kennedy Space Center (90 ft tall, holding ~ 730,000 gallons) was filled in 2025 to support Artemis II and subsequent flights (Fig.  24 ). Orion, the crew capsule, uses state-of-the-art proton-exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) or regenerative fuel cell (RFC) variants that produce electricity while generating water as a byproduct. For lunar surface operations, NASA and partners like Blue Origin are integrating gravity-independent fuel cells (e.g., Nimbus Power Systems technology) into the Blue Moon lander. These systems underwent successful shock and vibration testing in 2026, simulating launch loads for Artemis crewed landings[ 314 ]. Figure 24 Schematic illustration of future liquid hydrogen storage to Support Space Launch System.

Design and Development Highlights  The design of hydrogen systems for Artemis emphasizes safety, efficiency, and reliability in extreme environments. SLS cryogenic tanks are engineered with advanced insulation to minimize boil-off during ground operations and ascent. NASA introduced a new 1.4-million-gallon LH 2  sphere and improved loading procedures after Artemis I delays caused by hydrogen leaks at the tail service mast umbilical. Compared to those in the Apollo Program era, Orion’s fuel cells are smaller, more powerful, and more efficient (power-to-volume ratio) with much better heat control. During surface missions, regenerative fuel cells (RFCs) are being developed that can use electrolysis to store energy as hydrogen (H2) and oxygen (O2) while it is sunny, and convert this stored energy to electrical energy during periods of darkness or high demand. NASA’s Hydrogen Electrical Power System (HEPS) is focused on developing systems for supporting lunar habitats, while concepts for metal hydride storage systems are being explored to serve as small, safe, long-term reservoirs for hydrogen storage [ 315 ].

Extensive ground testing, including Wet Dress Rehearsals (WDRs) that test complete propellant loading and full countdowns, supports these development efforts. The partnership among Air Products (liquid hydrogen supplier), Nimbus (fuel cells), and Plug Power (additional cryogenic support) accelerates the development to market. Computer simulations and machine-learning applications have now been used to help develop the best methods for tank insulation, leak detection, and heat control, which will significantly reduce the costs of development [ 316 ].

Future Challenges in Space Missions . Although major progress has been achieved, there are still substantial challenges to operating deep space and maintaining sustainable operations on the Moon and Mars:

Cryogenic Handling and Leaks  Liquid hydrogen has an extreme temperature (-253 °C), which causes materials to shrink, seals to fail, and leaks to occur. Artemis II WDRs conducted in early 2026 again had to deal with leaking hydrogen caused by the hydrogen interfaces, which were an issue on Artemis I as well. The microgravity environment of space increases the boil-off rate of hydrogen and the separation of phases (liquid vs. vapor) [ 317 ].

Thermal Management in Vacuum  Fuel cell and energy storage devices release or consume heat. When deployed in outer space, radiative cooling becomes the only method, making thermal control essential. Regenerative fuel cells need to have electrolysis and electrical production be thermally compatible without the help of any infrastructure [ 318 ].

Long-Duration Storage and Mass Penalty  In case of long-duration missions, boil-off in LH2 becomes too much of a problem. Compact and reversible storage systems need to be developed. Metal hydrides have very high volumetric efficiency and are safe, but their gravimetric efficiency is very poor [ 319 ,  320 ].

Radiation and Material Degradation  Space radiation can cause embrittlement of the tank structure and membrane deterioration in fuel cells. Hydrogen permeation in composites becomes an issue for extended habitation periods [ 321 ].

In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU)  A sustainable future depends on the ability to extract hydrogen and oxygen from lunar ice. Electrolysis, liquefaction, and storage systems have to function independently under the challenging conditions of the Moon [ 322 ].

Scalability and Cost  As part of the Artemis program, NASA requires higher flight rates; reusable systems, advanced forms of thermal protection (e.g., variable density multilayer spacecraft heat shield material), and AI predictive maintenance standards must each contribute to lowering overall costs while still maintaining acceptable levels of safety [ 323 ].

Some of the ways NASA is approaching achieving the above goals are through the use of commercial research (e.g., the Regenerative Fuel Cell Project), BRACES (a program of Unitized Reversible Alkaline Cells), and partnerships to develop composite metal hydride/metal oxide frameworks for radiation shielding/storage. In addition, the transition from traditional Apollo-style consumable hydrogen/ oxygen fuel cells to solar regenerative systems demonstrates the shift toward closed-loop, sustainable propellant systems to achieve Artemis’s goals [ 324 ].

Hydrogen-based fuels remain critical to the propulsion and energy needs of Artemis. Advances in cryogenic engineering, fuel cell lifecycle testing, and new hydrogen storage options (i.e., metal hydrides) will be the keys to establishing a long-term human presence on the Moon and eventually conducting crewed missions to Mars.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The development of a viable hydrogen economy poses significant problems for hydrogen storage, and metal hydrides continue to hold promise in this regard. The present review explores four groups of metal hydrides, namely intermetallic, complex, magnesium, and chemical hydrides, and establishes that none of them fully satisfy the requirements for the perfect hydrogen storage material. They all have strengths and weaknesses in terms of gravimetric capacity, volumetric density, thermodynamic stability, kinetics, reversibility, safety, durability, and cost. Reversibility and good operating conditions are some of the strengths of intermetallic hydrides, while their main weakness lies in their low gravimetric capacity. Complex and chemical hydrides, on the other hand, have high hydrogen content despite having high desorption temperatures, poor kinetics, low reversibility, producing undesired products, or being difficult to regenerate.

It is worth noting that one important finding is that the performance of metal-hydride materials is a result of coupled thermodynamic and kinetic effects. The enthalpy, entropy, equilibrium plateau pressure, activation energy, diffusion distance, and phase equilibria are key factors responsible for hydrogen storage and release in real conditions. Pressure-composition-temperature diagrams, van’t Hoff analysis, and reaction kinetics are important in guiding the choice of materials and reactor designs. Success is dependent on methodologies to simultaneously manipulate energy landscapes and transport pathways. Nanostructuring leads to a reduction in diffusion distance, an improvement in transport by defects and grain boundaries, and a partial thermodynamic destabilization of the hydrides. Meanwhile, catalyst addition reduces the interfacial energy barrier for dissociation, diffusion, nucleation, and release processes.

The article concludes that beyond materials chemistry, there are other aspects that will determine the success of hydrogen storage. Future innovations such as high-entropy alloys, MOFs-containing designs, graphene-based systems, MXenes, and hybrids will enable multifunctionality where hydrogen storage is coupled with catalysis, heat transport, structural stability, and thermodynamic tuning all into one design. On the other hand, digital technologies such as AI, machine learning, and high-throughput screening are helping in the fast-tracking of innovation in this field by discovering potential materials and predicting their behavior through simulations.

The review connects scientific achievements with practical implementation. Commercial fuel cell electric vehicles provide an example of how hydrogen storage is moving from research to practice, where faster refueling, longer distances covered per charge, and reliable operation in cold weather have a distinct advantage in particular applications. Implementation highlights the necessity to consider hydrogen storage in combination with the development of supporting infrastructure, the cost of hydrogen production, and the economic viability of the system. The space missions of NASA and the Artemis program further demonstrate practical importance, proving that hydrogen storage plays an integral role in reducing emissions on Earth as well as sustaining human activity in space for extended periods of time.

Overall, the success of hydrogen storage relies not on improving each individual material but on integrated system optimization. In other words, the best storage systems in the future will combine all of these features, including high volumetric/gravimetric efficiency, operation at low pressure, heat generation management, longevity, minimal requirements for critical metals, and efficient manufacturing techniques. Future research should be directed toward earth-abundant and recyclable hydrides, a more fundamental understanding of interactions between hydrides and catalysts/interfaces, new hybrid storage solutions, both mobile and stationary, and materials that can operate under challenging conditions on Earth and in space.
